experience_rules.topic: Mechanics / Work-Energy Theorem and Conservation of Energy
experience_rules.title: 摩擦力做功累积性校验
experience_rules.trigger: 涉及往复运动或多阶段运动的能量守恒计算
experience_rules.check_logic: 摩擦力做功 Wf = -μmg * S_total，必须使用总路程 S 而非位移差 Δx。若预测结果出现位移项的一次幂与二次幂混合且符号不符合耗散逻辑，则存在建模错误。

experience_rules.topic: Mechanics / Work-Energy Theorem and Conservation of Energy
experience_rules.title: 物理量纲一致性检查
experience_rules.trigger: 得出最终物理公式或进行复杂代数化简后
experience_rules.check_logic: 检查等式两边的量纲是否一致。本题中周期 $T$ 的量纲应为 $[T]$，而预测结果 $\sqrt{mE}/A$ 的量纲为 $[M][L]/[F] = [T]^2$（错误），正确应为 $\sqrt{E/m}/A$。

experience_rules.topic: Mechanics / Work-Energy Theorem and Conservation of Energy
experience_rules.title: 根号内外因式化简校验
experience_rules.trigger: 将常数或变量移入/移出根号时
experience_rules.check_logic: 严格执行 $k\sqrt{x} = \sqrt{k^2 x}$。预测中将 $2$ 移入根号变为 $4$ 时，未注意分母上的 $2$ 抵消关系，且错误地翻转了 $m$ 的分子分母位置。

experience_rules.topic: Mechanics / Work-Energy Theorem and Conservation of Energy
experience_rules.title: 约束面运动速度分解校验
experience_rules.trigger: 物体在非平面约束（如抛物面、球面）上运动且涉及最高点计算

topics.topic: Moment of Inertia and Rotational Energy

top_down_rules.title: Verify rotational kinetic energy formula
top_down_rules.description: The rotational kinetic energy is given by the formula: KE_rot = (1/2)Ic9�b2, where I is the moment of inertia and c9 is the angular velocity. This equation applies to rigid bodies in rotation about a fixed axis.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the rotational kinetic energy is calculated using KE_rot = (1/2)Ic9�b2, and verify that I (moment of inertia) and c9 (angular velocity) are correctly identified, calculated, and used.
common_errors: Forgetting the (1/2) factor in the equation
Using linear velocity (v) instead of angular velocity (c9)
Incorrectly calculating or omitting the moment of inertia (I)

top_down_rules.title: Apply the parallel axis theorem correctly
top_down_rules.description: The parallel axis theorem states that I_total = I_cm + Md�b2, where I_cm is the moment of inertia about the center of mass, M is the mass of the object, and d is the distance from the axis of rotation to the center of mass.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify if the moment of inertia for an axis not passing through the center of mass is calculated using the parallel axis theorem. Ensure accurate values for d (distance) and M (mass) are used, and confirm that I_cm is correctly determined.
common_errors: Omitting the Md�b2 term when shifting the axis of rotation
Using the wrong distance (d) between the center of mass and the rotation axis
Confusing I_cm with I about the given axis

top_down_rules.title: Check perpendicular axis theorem application
top_down_rules.description: The perpendicular axis theorem states that for a planar object, I_z = I_x + I_y, where I_z is the moment of inertia about an axis perpendicular to the plane, and I_x and I_y are about axes in the plane. This is valid only for thin, planar objects.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure the perpendicular axis theorem is applied only to thin, planar objects. Verify that I_x and I_y are correctly calculated and summed to determine I_z, and confirm that the axes intersect at a single point.
common_errors: Applying the theorem to non-planar or 3D objects
Incorrectly summing I_x and I_y
Using the theorem when axes do not intersect at a single point

top_down_rules.title: Verify units of moment of inertia
top_down_rules.description: The moment of inertia (I) has the SI unit kg�b7m�b2, derived from the formula I = a mr�b2, where m is the mass and r is the distance. Consistency of units is critical in calculations.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Confirm that the final unit of I is kg�b7m�b2. Verify that all inputs (mass in kilograms, distance in meters) are in correct units, and ensure that the distance is squared (r�b2) when summing terms in I.
common_errors: Using incorrect units for mass or distance
Failing to square the distance (r�b2) when summing terms in I
Using inconsistent units (e.g., grams instead of kilograms)

top_down_rules.title: Check rotational energy conservation
top_down_rules.description: Rotational energy is conserved if there are no external torques acting on the system. This applies to isolated systems or systems with purely conservative internal forces.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify if external torques are zero. If yes, ensure the total rotational energy remains constant over time. Confirm that friction or other non-conservative forces are absent.
common_errors: Ignoring external torques that do work on the system
Assuming rotational energy conservation in the presence of friction
Confusing conservation of rotational energy with conservation of angular momentum

top_down_rules.title: Ensure correct sign convention for torque
top_down_rules.description: Torque (c4) is defined as c4 = r �d F = rFsin�3b8, where the direction is determined using the right-hand rule. Positive torque typically corresponds to counterclockwise rotation, and negative torque to clockwise rotation.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Confirm that the torque sign is determined using the right-hand rule and is consistent with the chosen coordinate system. Verify that the angle �3b8 is correctly used in c4 = rFsin�3b8.
common_errors: Reversing the sign convention for clockwise and counterclockwise torques
Neglecting the angle �3b8 in c4 = rFsin�3b8
Forgetting to use the cross product properly

top_down_rules.title: Verify geometric constraints in rotational systems
top_down_rules.description: In rotational mechanics, constraints like fixed radii or rigid body rotations must be respected. For example, all points on a rigid rotating disk have the same angular velocity but different linear velocities.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that angular velocity (c9) is constant across the rigid body and that linear velocity (v = rc9) is calculated appropriately for different points. Confirm that rigid body assumptions are not violated.
common_errors: Assuming linear velocity is the same for all points on a rigid body
Failing to account for the dependency of linear velocity on radius (v = rc9)
Applying non-rigid body assumptions to rigid systems

top_down_rules.title: Perform dimensional analysis for rotational energy equations
top_down_rules.description: The equations for rotational energy and moment of inertia must be dimensionally consistent. For example, KE_rot = (1/2)Ic9�b2 should result in units of energy (kg�b7m�b2/s�b2).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that each term in the rotational energy equation has compatible dimensions, and the final result has dimensions of energy (kg�b7m�b2/s�b2). Ensure that I and c9 are expressed in consistent units.
common_errors: Omitting or miscalculating the square of c9 in KE_rot = (1/2)Ic9�b2
Using inconsistent units for I or c9
Failing to check that the final energy has units of kg�b7m�b2/s�b2

top_down_rules.title: Verify angular momentum conservation
top_down_rules.description: Angular momentum is conserved in a system if there are no external torques acting on it. This principle applies to both rigid bodies and systems of particles.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that external torques are zero. If so, verify that the total angular momentum (L = Ic9) remains constant over time. Check that changes in I or c9 are consistent with conservation.
common_errors: Ignoring external torques that affect angular momentum
Assuming angular momentum conservation in the presence of friction or other non-conservative forces
Failing to account for changes in I or c9 when analyzing the system

topics.topic: Newton's Laws and Free Body Diagrams

top_down_rules.title: Verify Correct Form of Newton's Second Law
top_down_rules.description: Newton's Second Law states that the sum of the forces acting on an object must equal the mass of the object times its acceleration (ΣF = ma). This fundamental equation applies to any object with mass under the influence of forces.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the sum of forces is expressed as ΣF = ma, where 'm' is the object's mass and 'a' is its acceleration. Verify that all forces acting on the object are included in the summation.
common_errors: Mistaking weight for mass
Incorrectly isolating the acceleration component
Missing force components in the sum

top_down_rules.title: Ensure Consistent Sign Convention in Coordinate Systems
top_down_rules.description: Whenever forces and accelerations are resolved into components along coordinate axes (e.g., x, y), it is essential to maintain consistent sign conventions (e.g., right and up are positive).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that forces and accelerations align with the chosen coordinate system sign conventions throughout the problem. Ensure that the positive and negative directions are clearly defined and consistently applied.
common_errors: Inconsistent sign usage for forces along different axes
Not defining the positive direction
Switching axes without redefining direction

top_down_rules.title: Check Vertical Geometric Constraints
top_down_rules.description: Geometric constraints can enforce conditions like an object must remain on a surface. For vertical scenarios, tension in a rope or normal force on a surface typically counteracts weight.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the normal force or tension balances vertical forces as per the defined constraint (e.g., no net vertical acceleration if stationary on a surface). Verify that the forces satisfy the geometric constraints of the problem.
common_errors: Neglect of normal forces when an object is on a surface
Incorrect calculation of tension
Ignoring constraints like fixed surfaces or ropes

top_down_rules.title: Confirm Conditions for Newton's Laws Application
top_down_rules.description: Newton's Laws can only be applied in inertial frames of reference where no acceleration or rotation affects the observer, and forces must be real at macroscopic scale.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the problem defines or implies an inertial reference frame. If the frame is non-inertial, ensure pseudo-forces are included to account for the effects of acceleration or rotation.
common_errors: Applying laws without considering inertial frames
Forgetting to account for pseudo-forces in non-inertial reference frames
Misidentifying the frame of reference

top_down_rules.title: Ensure Dimensional Consistency for Forces
top_down_rules.description: In mechanics, forces must be measured in units consistent with mass times acceleration (e.g., Newtons in SI units). Dimensional analysis ensures all terms in an equation balance correctly.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that all force and acceleration terms have units consistent with Newtons (kg·m/s²) in SI. Ensure that unit conversions, if any, are correctly applied.
common_errors: Using incorrect units for mass or acceleration
Inconsistent unit usage among different force components
Forgetting to convert units when necessary

top_down_rules.title: Check Action-Reaction Force Pairs
top_down_rules.description: Newton's Third Law states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction, meaning forces always occur in pairs between two interacting bodies.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that every force has a corresponding equal and opposite reaction force, typically between two interacting bodies in isolation. Ensure that the forces act on different objects and are of the same magnitude but opposite in direction.
common_errors: Forgetting to include or identify reaction forces
Misidentifying action-reaction force pairs
Confusing internal forces with action-reaction pairs

top_down_rules.title: Differentiate Between External and Internal Forces
top_down_rules.description: For solving and analyzing systems with Newton's Laws, it's crucial to identify external forces acting on a system as distinct from internal forces acting among components in the system.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Differentiate and correctly label external forces versus internal forces in system analysis. Ensure that only external forces are included in the equations of motion for the system as a whole.
common_errors: Confusing internal with external forces
Neglecting to include external forces in equations of motion
Incorrectly summing internal forces in system-level analysis

top_down_rules.title: Analyze Friction Forces
top_down_rules.description: Frictional forces oppose the relative motion or tendency of motion between two surfaces in contact. Static friction prevents motion up to a maximum value, while kinetic friction acts during motion.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that frictional forces are correctly identified and calculated using the appropriate coefficients of friction (static or kinetic). Ensure that static friction does not exceed its maximum value (μsN).
common_errors: Using the wrong coefficient of friction
Exceeding the maximum static friction force
Neglecting frictional forces in the analysis

top_down_rules.title: Verify Net Force for Equilibrium
top_down_rules.description: For an object in equilibrium, the net force acting on it must be zero. This applies to both static equilibrium (no motion) and dynamic equilibrium (constant velocity).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the sum of all forces acting on the object is zero in both the horizontal and vertical directions. Verify that there is no net acceleration.
common_errors: Forgetting to include all forces in the summation
Incorrectly resolving forces into components
Assuming equilibrium without verifying net force

topics.topic: Non-inertial Reference Frames and Pseudo Forces

top_down_rules.title: Apply pseudo force in non-inertial frames
top_down_rules.description: In a non-inertial reference frame, an additional pseudo force must be introduced to account for the observed motion. The pseudo force is given by F_pseudo = -m * a_frame, where m is the mass of the object and a_frame is the acceleration of the non-inertial frame.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify if a pseudo force has been correctly added with the magnitude (-m * a_frame) and direction (opposite to the frame's acceleration).
common_errors: Omitting the pseudo force in calculations.
Using incorrect magnitude or sign for the pseudo force.
Confusing the pseudo force direction with the frame acceleration direction.

top_down_rules.title: Modify Newton's second law in non-inertial frames
top_down_rules.description: Newton's second law (F_net = m * a) must be modified in a non-inertial reference frame by including the pseudo force. The equation becomes: F_net + F_pseudo = m * a_observed.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the pseudo force is included in the net force equation, and the observed acceleration is used in calculations.
common_errors: Using the inertial acceleration instead of the observed acceleration.
Failing to add the pseudo force term in the net force equation.

top_down_rules.title: Ensure correct sign convention for pseudo force
top_down_rules.description: The pseudo force always acts opposite to the acceleration of the non-inertial reference frame. This sign convention must be adhered to for correct results.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the pseudo force direction is opposite to the acceleration of the reference frame.
common_errors: Assigning the pseudo force in the same direction as the reference frame's acceleration.
Inconsistent application of sign conventions in calculations.

top_down_rules.title: Use consistent coordinate system in non-inertial frames
top_down_rules.description: When solving problems in non-inertial frames, the chosen coordinate system (e.g., Cartesian or polar) must remain consistent throughout the calculation, and the pseudo force must be expressed in the same system.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that all forces, accelerations, and pseudo forces are resolved consistently within the chosen coordinate system.
common_errors: Switching between coordinate systems mid-calculation without transformation.
Failing to resolve pseudo force components into the chosen coordinate system.

top_down_rules.title: Account for geometric constraints in non-inertial frames
top_down_rules.description: In problems involving non-inertial frames, any geometric constraints (e.g., objects on inclined planes, pendulum motion) must also include the effects of pseudo forces.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that pseudo forces are included when analyzing forces and accelerations along constrained paths.
common_errors: Ignoring pseudo forces when applying geometric constraints.
Incorrect resolution of pseudo forces along the constrained directions.

top_down_rules.title: Include Coriolis force in rotating reference frames
top_down_rules.description: In rotating reference frames, the Coriolis force must be included. It is given by F_coriolis = -2m(ω × v), where ω is the angular velocity of the frame and v is the velocity of the object relative to the rotating frame.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the Coriolis force is included with the correct magnitude and direction using the cross product formula.
common_errors: Forgetting to include the Coriolis force in rotating frames.
Using incorrect cross product order for ω and v.
Incorrectly calculating the magnitude or direction of the Coriolis force.

top_down_rules.title: Include centrifugal force in rotating reference frames
top_down_rules.description: In a rotating reference frame, the centrifugal force must be included. It is given by F_centrifugal = -mω²r, where r is the radial distance of the object from the axis of rotation.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the centrifugal force is included with the correct magnitude and direction (outward from the axis of rotation).
common_errors: Omitting the centrifugal force in rotating frames.
Using the wrong direction for the centrifugal force (should be radially outward).
Incorrectly calculating the radial distance or angular velocity.

top_down_rules.title: Ensure dimensional consistency in pseudo force equations
top_down_rules.description: In equations involving pseudo forces, ensure that all terms have consistent dimensions. For example, pseudo force should have units of force (e.g., Newtons in SI).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check that the dimensions of all terms in the pseudo force equation are consistent (e.g., mass × acceleration results in force).
common_errors: Using incorrect units for mass or acceleration in pseudo force calculations.
Adding terms with inconsistent dimensions (e.g., mixing force and acceleration).

top_down_rules.title: Verify equation of motion consistency for coupled systems
top_down_rules.description: Ensure that the equations of motion for each oscillator in the coupled system are correctly derived using Newton’s second law or the Lagrangian method. The coupling force should be properly included.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the second-order differential equations correctly include restoring forces, coupling forces, and damping (if specified). Ensure that the spring constants, masses, and displacements match the problem setup and that the coupling force is derived based on relative displacements.
common_errors: Omitting the coupling force in the equations of motion.
Incorrect sign for the restoring force or coupling terms.
Forgetting to account for the displacement of both masses in the coupling term.

top_down_rules.title: Check validity of superposition principle
top_down_rules.description: In normal modes, displacements are assumed to be linear combinations of eigenfunctions. This principle applies only when the system is linear and the coupling forces follow Hooke's Law.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure the problem setup specifies linear restoring forces and that no nonlinear terms (e.g., cubic or higher-order terms) are introduced in the equations of motion. Verify that the coupling forces are proportional to displacement.
common_errors: Using superposition principle in a nonlinear system.
Including cubic or higher-order terms in the coupling or restoring forces, which invalidates normal mode analysis.

top_down_rules.title: Verify normal mode frequencies are correctly determined
top_down_rules.description: The frequencies of the normal modes are the eigenvalues of the system matrix derived from the equations of motion. These must be calculated correctly using a determinant or matrix diagonalization technique.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check that the determinant of the matrix (Mω² - K) is set to zero for eigenvalue calculation. Ensure that the square root of eigenvalues is taken to find angular frequencies and that the units of mass and spring constants are consistent.
common_errors: Forgetting to set the determinant to zero.
Incorrectly calculating the eigenvalues of the system matrix.
Using incorrect units or dimensions for mass or spring constants, leading to wrong frequency values.

top_down_rules.title: Check adherence to sign conventions for displacement and force directions
top_down_rules.description: Ensure that all displacements, forces, and coupling terms follow a consistent sign convention. For example, a displacement to the right should correspond to a positive restoring force to the left.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that force terms in the equations of motion have the correct signs based on the chosen coordinate system and direction of displacement. Ensure consistency across all oscillators in the system.
common_errors: Using inconsistent sign conventions for different oscillators.
Forgetting to reverse the sign of the force when the displacement is in the opposite direction.
Ignoring the effect of the coupling spring, leading to mismatched signs in the coupling term.

top_down_rules.title: Verify proper application of initial conditions
top_down_rules.description: Initial conditions (initial displacements and velocities) should be applied consistently to solve for the time-dependent motion of the system. These conditions determine the amplitudes and phases of the modes.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the initial conditions are substituted into the general solution correctly to solve for constants of integration. Verify that the initial conditions are applied to all oscillators in the system.
common_errors: Forgetting to apply initial conditions to both oscillators in a coupled system.
Incorrect substitution of initial displacement or velocity values into the general solution.
Mistaking the initial phase for initial velocity or vice versa.

top_down_rules.title: Check geometric constraints in coupled oscillator systems
top_down_rules.description: Some systems have geometric constraints (e.g., fixed total length of a string or rod). These constraints must be incorporated into the equations of motion.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the sum of displacements satisfies the geometric constraint, if specified (e.g., x1 + x2 = constant for a fixed-length system). Ensure that the constraint is used to reduce the number of independent variables in the system.
common_errors: Ignoring the geometric constraint altogether.
Misinterpreting the constraint equation, leading to incorrect coupling terms.
Forgetting to reduce the number of independent variables based on the constraint.

top_down_rules.title: Check dimensional consistency of all terms
top_down_rules.description: Ensure that all terms in the equations of motion and derived quantities (frequencies, displacements) have consistent dimensions. For example, frequencies must have dimensions of [T^-1].
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify unit consistency in each term of the equations of motion. Check that frequencies are derived with proper units based on the spring constant and mass. Ensure that all derived quantities maintain dimensional consistency.
common_errors: Using inconsistent units for spring constants (e.g., N/m vs. N/mm).
Forgetting to convert mass or displacement units, leading to incorrect frequency calculations.
Failing to ensure all terms in the equation of motion are dimensionally consistent.

top_down_rules.title: Verify mode orthogonality
top_down_rules.description: In coupled oscillation systems, the eigenvectors (modes) should be orthogonal with respect to the mass matrix. This property arises from the symmetry of the system.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check that the dot product of eigenvectors (using the mass matrix as a weighting factor) is zero for distinct modes. Ensure that the system matrix is symmetric or Hermitian, as required for orthogonality.
common_errors: Incorrectly calculating the eigenvectors, leading to loss of orthogonality.
Omitting the mass matrix in the orthogonality check.
Assuming orthogonality in a non-symmetric or non-Hermitian system, where it may not hold.

top_down_rules.title: Verify energy consistency in normal modes
top_down_rules.description: The total energy of the system should be conserved in the absence of damping. The energy should be correctly distributed among kinetic and potential components for each mode.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the total energy (sum of kinetic and potential energy) remains constant over time for undamped systems. Verify that the energy expressions for each mode are consistent with the displacements and velocities.
common_errors: Forgetting to include both kinetic and potential energy terms.
Incorrectly calculating the potential energy due to coupling forces.
Failing to verify energy conservation in undamped systems.

top_down_rules.title: Verify Angular Frequency and Linear Frequency Relationship
top_down_rules.description: For Simple Harmonic Motion, angular frequency ω is related to linear frequency f by ω = 2πf. This relationship is fundamental for oscillatory systems.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure ω = 2πf is used correctly in calculations relating angular frequency and linear frequency, and verify unit consistency (e.g., radians per second for ω and hertz for f).
common_errors: Incorrect conversion factor between ω and f
Using linear frequency instead of angular frequency in equations

top_down_rules.title: Check Energy Conservation in SHM Systems
top_down_rules.description: In ideal Simple Harmonic Motion, mechanical energy is conserved. The sum of kinetic and potential energy in the system remains constant.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify if E_total = E_kinetic + E_potential remains constant over time, and ensure proper expressions for kinetic energy (1/2 mv²) and potential energy (1/2 kx²) are used.
common_errors: Ignoring potential energy contributions near maximum displacement
Forgetting kinetic energy at equilibrium position
Incorrect expressions for energy terms

top_down_rules.title: Validate Position and Velocity Equations for Spring-Mass Systems
top_down_rules.description: Position x(t) and velocity v(t) of a mass on a spring are given by x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ) and v(t) = -Aω sin(ωt + φ), where A is amplitude and φ is the phase constant.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that position and velocity equations are correctly applied with proper amplitude, angular frequency, and phase constants. Ensure units are consistent and trigonometric functions are correctly evaluated.
common_errors: Incorrect sign for velocity expression
Misidentifying amplitude or missing phase shift
Using incorrect angular frequency in equations

top_down_rules.title: Ensure Correct Sign Convention for Forces and Displacements
top_down_rules.description: In SHM, the restoring force is typically considered negative in direction opposite to displacement (F = -kx for spring systems).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check that restoring forces are consistently negative when displacements are positive, and verify that Hooke's Law is applied correctly.
common_errors: Misinterpretation of force directions
Incorrect sign usage when applying Hooke's Law
Confusion between restoring force and applied force

top_down_rules.title: Verify Validity Conditions for SHM Applicability
top_down_rules.description: SHM applies in systems where net restoring forces are proportional to displacement and damping forces are negligible.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure system criteria such as linear restoring force proportionality (e.g., Hooke's Law) and negligible damping are met. Verify that the system is not influenced by external forces or significant non-linearities.
common_errors: Applying SHM principles in non-linear force systems
Ignoring damping effects which invalidate ideal SHM assumption
Overlooking external forces affecting the system

top_down_rules.title: Ensure Dimensional Consistency in SHM Equations
top_down_rules.description: All equations in SHM should be dimensionally consistent. Units must balance, specifically for ω, x(t), and v(t).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if each term in equations maintains consistent dimensions, particularly length [L], time [T], and mass [M]. Ensure angular frequency is in radians per second, position in meters, and velocity in meters per second.
common_errors: Using incorrect units for angular frequency
Mixing units inconsistently in calculations
Overlooking dimensional consistency in derived equations

top_down_rules.title: Validate Period-Time Relation in Oscillations
top_down_rules.description: The period T of a mass-spring oscillator is calculated as T = 2π√(m/k). This applies under ideal conditions of simple harmonic oscillators.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify whether the calculated period matches T = 2π√(m/k) using the correct formula, proper unit conversion, and accurate values for mass and spring constant.
common_errors: Incorrect physical constant usage
Using period formulas outside applicable contexts
Neglecting unit consistency in mass or spring constant

top_down_rules.title: Check for Phase Shift Due to Damping in Real Oscillators
top_down_rules.description: Real-world oscillators may exhibit phase shifts due to damping forces. Evaluate phase changes in the presence of damping.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Determine if phase shifts have been correctly factored into calculations where damping is present. Verify that the damping coefficient and its effect on the phase constant are accurately considered.
common_errors: Ignoring phase shift in damped systems
Incorrect adjustment of phase constant in damped scenarios
Overlooking the relationship between damping and angular frequency

top_down_rules.title: Verify Initial Conditions for SHM Systems
top_down_rules.description: Initial conditions, such as initial displacement and velocity, determine the phase constant and amplitude in SHM equations.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that initial conditions are correctly applied to determine the phase constant φ and amplitude A. Verify that x(0) and v(0) are consistent with the given equations.
common_errors: Incorrectly calculating phase constant from initial conditions
Ignoring initial velocity or displacement in calculations
Using inconsistent initial conditions in equations

experience_rules.topic: Oscillations and Simple Harmonic Motion
experience_rules.title: 复杂振动系统等效质量法
experience_rules.trigger: 系统包含平动质量、转动惯量及多个弹性元件时
experience_rules.check_logic: 通过能量守恒 E = 1/2 * M_eff * v^2 + 1/2 * K_eff * x^2 = const，求导得出周期 T = 2π√(M_eff/K_eff)，确保 M_eff 包含所有动能项的转化。

experience_rules.topic: Oscillations and Simple Harmonic Motion
experience_rules.title: 滑轮组位移约束校验
experience_rules.trigger: 题目提及“保持水平”、“不伸长绳索”及“滑轮”
experience_rules.check_logic: 检查各弹性元件的形变量与中心位移的几何关系是否满足位移协调方程，不可盲目假设各支路位移相等。

top_down_rules.title: Verify Power is the Dot Product of Force and Velocity
top_down_rules.description: Power is calculated as the dot product of the force vector and the velocity vector of the object. This assumes the force and velocity are expressed in the same coordinate system.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure Power P = F · v = F_x*v_x + F_y*v_y + F_z*v_z, where F and v are vectors in the same coordinate system.
common_errors: Using scalar multiplication instead of dot product
Ignoring directional components of force and velocity
Using mismatched coordinate systems for force and velocity

top_down_rules.title: Check Conservation of Energy with Dissipative Forces
top_down_rules.description: When dissipative forces like friction are present, mechanical energy is not conserved. Energy is transformed into heat or other forms of non-mechanical energy.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify if E_final = E_initial - work_done_by_dissipative_forces, where work_done_by_dissipative_forces accounts for friction, air resistance, or other non-conservative forces.
common_errors: Forgetting to subtract work done by friction from total energy
Incorrectly assuming mechanical energy is conserved in the presence of friction
Failing to account for all forms of dissipative forces

top_down_rules.title: Ensure Mechanical Energy Dimensional Consistency
top_down_rules.description: Mechanical energy equations must adhere to dimensional consistency, ensuring all terms relating to energy are expressed in Joules.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that all energy terms have units consistent with kg·m^2/s^2 (Joules) and that unit conversions are correctly applied.
common_errors: Using conflicting units for energy calculations
Omitting proper conversion between units
Mixing incompatible unit systems (e.g., SI and imperial)

top_down_rules.title: Validate Power Calculation Over Time
top_down_rules.description: Power is the rate of energy transfer over time. For scenarios involving energy changes, power is calculated as the derivative of energy with respect to time.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure P = dE/dt, where E is the total energy including potential, kinetic, and work done. Verify that the time derivative is correctly computed.
common_errors: Ignoring rate of change of energy over time
Calculating power without considering energy changes over time
Misinterpreting the derivative of energy with respect to time

top_down_rules.title: Confirm Correct Sign Convention in Calculations
top_down_rules.description: Power and energy equations are sensitive to the sign convention used in the coordinate system. Ensure consistent use of positive and negative signs based on component directions.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the sign convention is consistent across all calculations, particularly for forces and motion directions that contribute positively or negatively to power.
common_errors: Inconsistent sign usage leading to incorrect power calculation
Missing negative sign in calculations involving resistance forces like friction
Using conflicting sign conventions in different parts of the calculation

top_down_rules.title: Ensure Dynamic Conditions for Accurate Power Analysis
top_down_rules.description: Power analysis requires objects to be moving. Static cases with zero velocity should not involve power calculations linked to kinetic aspects.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Confirm that velocity v ≠ 0 for legitimate power calculation. If v = 0, ensure power is not attributed to kinetic energy transfer.
common_errors: Calculating power for static cases where object velocity is zero
Ignoring the need for motion in assessing power
Misinterpreting static forces as contributing to power

top_down_rules.title: Identify Misapplications of Frictionless Power Assumptions
top_down_rules.description: In scenarios with significant friction, assumptions that power can be transferred through frictionless work are invalid.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that frictional forces are accounted for in power calculations, especially in systems where friction is non-negligible.
common_errors: Assuming frictionless conditions in a friction-present scenario
Excluding friction from work calculations leading to power
Underestimating the impact of friction on energy dissipation

top_down_rules.title: Assess Geometric Constraints in Energy Calculations
top_down_rules.description: Energy calculations involving geometric constraints such as inclines or curves must consider the modified forces and resulting work/energy changes.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that geometric parameters like angle of incline, curvature, or path constraints are accounted for in energy formulations.
common_errors: Neglecting incline angles in potential energy and work calculations
Using straight path assumptions in geometrically constrained problems
Ignoring the effect of curvature on energy dissipation or work

top_down_rules.title: Validate Work-Energy Theorem Application
top_down_rules.description: The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on an object is equal to its change in kinetic energy. Ensure this principle is correctly applied.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that W_net = ΔK = K_final - K_initial, where W_net is the total work done by all forces.
common_errors: Ignoring contributions of all forces to net work
Miscalculating changes in kinetic energy
Applying the theorem incorrectly in non-inertial reference frames

top_down_rules.title: Ensure Correct Reference Point for Potential Energy
top_down_rules.description: Potential energy calculations depend on the choice of a reference point. Ensure the reference point is clearly defined and consistently used.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the reference point for potential energy (e.g., height = 0) is explicitly stated and consistently applied in calculations.
common_errors: Using inconsistent reference points for potential energy
Failing to define a reference point in energy problems
Misinterpreting relative potential energy differences

top_down_rules.title: Verify equations of motion for horizontal and vertical components
top_down_rules.description: In projectile motion, the horizontal motion is constant (no acceleration), while the vertical motion is uniformly accelerated due to gravity. The horizontal displacement is given by x = v_x * t, and the vertical displacement is given by y = v_y * t - (1/2) * g * t^2.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure horizontal motion uses x = v_x * t, and vertical motion uses y = v_y * t - (1/2) * g * t^2 without errors in terms, coefficients, or signs. Confirm that g is positive in magnitude and applied with the correct sign based on the chosen coordinate system.
common_errors: Using acceleration in the horizontal motion equation
Missing the (1/2) factor in the vertical displacement formula
Incorrect sign for the gravitational term (-g * t^2)

top_down_rules.title: Check adherence to consistent sign conventions
top_down_rules.description: In projectile motion, a consistent coordinate system is required. For example, upward is typically positive and downward (gravity) is negative. Horizontal directions should also have consistent signs (e.g., +x for rightward).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that gravity (g) is given a negative sign if upward is positive and that horizontal displacements/velocities are consistent with the chosen coordinate system. Ensure that all components of motion adhere to the same convention throughout the problem.
common_errors: Assigning gravity a positive value when upward is positive
Inconsistent signs for initial vertical velocity and acceleration due to gravity
Mixing up left/right or up/down conventions in calculations

top_down_rules.title: Validate range formula for horizontal displacement
top_down_rules.description: The horizontal range of a projectile is given by R = (v_0^2 * sin(2θ)) / g, assuming launch and landing heights are the same. This formula only applies under this condition.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check that the condition of equal launch and landing heights is met before applying R = (v_0^2 * sin(2θ)) / g. If the heights differ, ensure the range is calculated using the appropriate kinematic equations.
common_errors: Using the range formula when the projectile lands at a different height than the launch height
Incorrectly substituting angle θ (e.g., using sin(θ) instead of sin(2θ))
Forgetting to square the initial velocity (v_0^2)

top_down_rules.title: Ensure correct time of flight calculation
top_down_rules.description: The total time of flight for a projectile launched and landing at the same height is given by T = (2 * v_0 * sin(θ)) / g. If launch and landing heights differ, a quadratic equation must be solved.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify use of T = (2 * v_0 * sin(θ)) / g only when launch and landing heights are equal. For differing heights, ensure a quadratic equation is solved for time, and confirm that the correct root of the equation is used.
common_errors: Using the symmetric time of flight formula when launch and landing heights are different
Missing the factor of 2 in the symmetric time of flight equation
Incorrectly solving the quadratic equation for unequal heights

top_down_rules.title: Verify decomposition of initial velocity into components
top_down_rules.description: The initial velocity vector (v_0) must be broken into horizontal (v_x = v_0 * cos(θ)) and vertical (v_y = v_0 * sin(θ)) components based on the launch angle θ.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure horizontal and vertical velocity components are correctly calculated using trigonometric functions and the launch angle. Confirm that the angle is in the correct unit (radians or degrees) as required by the trigonometric functions.
common_errors: Using sin(θ) instead of cos(θ) for the horizontal component
Using cos(θ) instead of sin(θ) for the vertical component
Incorrect angle input (e.g., degrees instead of radians without conversion)

top_down_rules.title: Confirm correct calculation of maximum height
top_down_rules.description: The maximum height of a projectile is reached when the vertical velocity becomes zero. It is given by H = (v_0^2 * sin^2(θ)) / (2 * g).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check that H = (v_0^2 * sin^2(θ)) / (2 * g) is used to calculate the maximum height and that the vertical velocity is zero at this point. Ensure sin^2(θ) is calculated correctly and that g is positive in magnitude.
common_errors: Incorrect use of sin^2(θ) (e.g., using sin(θ) instead of squaring the term)
Forgetting to divide by 2g
Assuming maximum height occurs at T/2 without verifying symmetry

top_down_rules.title: Perform dimensional and unit consistency check
top_down_rules.description: All equations in projectile motion must be dimensionally consistent. For example, displacement must have units of length, time must have units of seconds, and g must have units of m/s^2.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that all terms in the equations have consistent units and dimensions. For example, check that g is in m/s^2 and time is in seconds. Verify that trigonometric functions are dimensionless and that derived quantities have the correct units.
common_errors: Using inconsistent units for g (e.g., cm/s^2 instead of m/s^2)
Mismatched units for displacement (e.g., mixing meters and centimeters)
Incorrect dimensional analysis leading to invalid terms in equations

top_down_rules.title: Check validity conditions for projectile motion assumptions
top_down_rules.description: Projectile motion assumes no air resistance, a constant gravitational field, and motion near the Earth's surface. These assumptions must hold for the equations to be valid.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the problem assumes no air resistance and that the motion occurs in a uniform gravitational field near the Earth's surface. Confirm that the effects of Earth's curvature or Coriolis forces are negligible.
common_errors: Ignoring air resistance in situations where it is significant
Applying projectile motion equations in non-uniform gravitational fields
Extending results to cases where Earth's curvature or Coriolis effects are significant

top_down_rules.title: Verify initial conditions for projectile motion
top_down_rules.description: The initial velocity, angle, and position must be clearly defined and consistent with the problem setup. These values are critical for accurate calculations.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the initial velocity, angle, and position are explicitly stated and used consistently in all calculations. Verify that the angle is measured from the horizontal and that the initial position is correctly incorporated into displacement equations.
common_errors: Omitting the initial position in displacement calculations
Using an incorrect reference for the launch angle
Inconsistent or undefined initial velocity values

top_down_rules.title: Verify relative velocity equation
top_down_rules.description: The relative velocity between two objects A and B is given by v_AB = v_A - v_B. This principle applies when the velocities are measured in the same inertial reference frame.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the relative velocity computation follows the vector subtraction v_AB = v_A - v_B, where all velocity vectors are expressed in the same coordinate system.
common_errors: Using addition instead of subtraction for relative velocity
Mixing up the order of subtraction (v_AB should be v_A - v_B, not v_B - v_A)
Using incompatible coordinate systems for velocity components

top_down_rules.title: Ensure consistency in sign conventions
top_down_rules.description: In relative motion problems, consistent sign conventions must be used for all velocity components. For example, positive x-direction is typically to the right, and positive y-direction is upward.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that all velocity components adhere to the same sign convention throughout the solution, and document any justified deviations clearly.
common_errors: Inconsistent sign conventions for velocity components (e.g., mixing positive and negative directions arbitrarily)
Reversing the sign of one component without justification
Failing to adjust signs when switching to a new reference frame

top_down_rules.title: Check proper switching between reference frames
top_down_rules.description: When switching between reference frames, relative velocities must be transformed correctly using the equation v_A_in_B = v_A_in_C - v_B_in_C, where C is the common reference frame.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that switching between reference frames uses the correct vector subtraction and that all vectors are expressed in the same coordinate system before transformation.
common_errors: Failing to identify the common reference frame correctly
Neglecting to subtract the velocity of the reference frame
Incorrectly assuming velocities are independent of the reference frame

top_down_rules.title: Ensure dimensional consistency in velocity calculations
top_down_rules.description: All terms in relative velocity equations must have consistent units, typically meters per second (m/s) in SI units. This ensures dimensional accuracy.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that all velocity terms have the same units and dimensions before performing any operations (e.g., subtraction or addition).
common_errors: Using inconsistent units for velocities (e.g., m/s for one term and km/h for another)
Failing to convert units to a consistent system before calculations
Mixing dimensional quantities (e.g., adding a velocity and a displacement)

top_down_rules.title: Apply geometric constraints for relative motion
top_down_rules.description: In problems involving constrained motion (e.g., objects connected by a rope), the relative motion between objects must satisfy the geometric constraints imposed by the system (e.g., constant rope length).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the relative velocities or displacements satisfy the geometric constraints (e.g., sum of displacements equals rope length).
common_errors: Ignoring the length constraint for connected objects
Incorrectly assigning relative velocities that violate the geometric constraint
Failing to consider the impact of pulleys on relative motion

top_down_rules.title: Check validity of kinematic equations for relative motion
top_down_rules.description: Kinematic equations for relative motion are valid only under uniform acceleration or constant velocity conditions in inertial reference frames.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that relative motion equations are applied only in scenarios of constant acceleration or velocity, and ensure the reference frame is inertial.
common_errors: Applying kinematic equations in non-inertial frames without accounting for pseudo-forces
Using kinematic equations in scenarios with variable acceleration
Assuming all reference frames are inertial without verification

top_down_rules.title: Verify relative acceleration relationship
top_down_rules.description: The relative acceleration between two objects A and B is given by a_AB = a_A - a_B. This applies in an inertial reference frame where accelerations are measured relative to a common origin.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that relative acceleration is calculated using vector subtraction a_AB = a_A - a_B, with proper consideration of the coordinate system.
common_errors: Mixing up the order of subtraction (a_AB should be a_A - a_B, not a_B - a_A)
Neglecting to account for direction when subtracting acceleration vectors
Using non-inertial reference frames without proper adjustments

top_down_rules.title: Ensure correct calculation of relative displacement
top_down_rules.description: Relative displacement between two objects A and B is given by s_AB = s_A - s_B, where both s_A and s_B are measured from the same reference point.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that relative displacement calculations use vector subtraction and that all displacements are measured with respect to the same origin.
common_errors: Using addition instead of subtraction for relative displacement
Mixing up the order of subtraction (s_AB should be s_A - s_B, not s_B - s_A)
Failing to specify or use a common reference point for displacement measurements

top_down_rules.title: Consider the impact of angles on relative motion
top_down_rules.description: In problems involving relative motion with angular components, ensure correct consideration of angles, using trigonometric relationships to resolve velocity and displacement into components.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Confirm that angles are correctly used to resolve vectors into components, with correct application of trigonometric functions and consistent units (e.g., radians or degrees).
common_errors: Incorrectly resolving velocity or displacement vectors without regard to angles
Using incorrect trigonometric functions based on angle orientation (e.g., sine versus cosine)
Failing to convert angle units consistently when necessary

top_down_rules.title: Verify the resonance condition for driving frequency
top_down_rules.description: The resonance condition occurs when the driving frequency matches the natural frequency of the system. For a harmonic oscillator, this is given by ω_d = ω_0, where ω_d is the driving frequency, and ω_0 = sqrt(k/m) is the natural frequency.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the driving frequency (ω_d) equals the natural frequency (ω_0 = sqrt(k/m)).
common_errors: Using an incorrect expression for the natural frequency, e.g., forgetting the square root.
Confusing angular frequency (ω) with linear frequency (f) by not using ω = 2πf.
Not accounting for the mass (m) or spring constant (k) in ω_0.

top_down_rules.title: Verify the equation of motion for damped oscillations
top_down_rules.description: The equation of motion for damped oscillations is m(d²x/dt²) + b(dx/dt) + kx = 0, where b is the damping coefficient.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify the presence and correct expression of the inertial force (m(d²x/dt²)), damping force (b(dx/dt)), and restoring force (kx).
common_errors: Omitting the damping term (b(dx/dt)).
Using incorrect sign conventions (e.g., wrong signs for forces).
Failing to include the mass (m) in the inertial term.

top_down_rules.title: Verify boundary and initial conditions for oscillations
top_down_rules.description: Ensure the initial displacement and velocity are correctly applied to the solution of the damped or driven oscillation equation.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if initial conditions (e.g., x(0) and dx/dt|_(t=0)) are correctly substituted into the differential equation solution.
common_errors: Using incorrect or arbitrary initial conditions.
Misinterpreting the initial velocity as initial displacement.
Failing to consistently apply initial conditions across all terms.

top_down_rules.title: Verify energy dissipation in damped oscillations
top_down_rules.description: In damped oscillations, total mechanical energy decreases over time due to the damping force. The energy at any time is E(t) = (1/2)m(dx/dt)² + (1/2)kx², decreasing monotonically.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure E(t) is correctly computed and decreases over time for a damped oscillator.
common_errors: Forgetting to include kinetic or potential energy terms in E(t).
Not accounting for the work done by the damping force.
Using an incorrect sign for energy dissipation.

top_down_rules.title: Verify consistent sign conventions for forces and displacements
top_down_rules.description: In oscillatory motion, restoring forces oppose displacement and damping forces oppose velocity.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure restoring force is -kx and damping force is -b(dx/dt), using negative signs to indicate opposition.
common_errors: Assigning a positive sign to the restoring force.
Reversing the direction of the damping force.
Inconsistent sign conventions across terms in the equation.

top_down_rules.title: Verify dimensional consistency of equations
top_down_rules.description: Confirm that all terms in the equation have dimensions of force (ML/T²). Check m(d²x/dt²), b(dx/dt), and kx.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that each term has dimensions of force. Mass should be M, damping coefficient should be ML/T, and spring constant should be ML/T².
common_errors: Using incorrect units for mass, damping coefficient, or spring constant.
Failing to ensure consistency between angular frequency and linear frequency.
Neglecting the time squared factor in acceleration terms.

top_down_rules.title: Verify validity conditions for resonance and damping equations
top_down_rules.description: Ensure assumptions like small oscillations, linear restoring forces, and negligible perturbations hold.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if oscillations are small, restoring force follows Hooke's Law, and nonlinear effects are minimal.
common_errors: Applying equations to large oscillations where linearity fails.
Neglecting external non-conservative forces affecting the system.
Assuming Hooke's Law holds for non-linear springs.

top_down_rules.title: Verify calculation of the quality factor (Q)
top_down_rules.description: The quality factor (Q) quantifies resonance sharpness, given by Q = ω_0/(2β), where β = b/(2m).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Calculate Q using Q = ω_0/(2β), ensuring β = b/(2m).
common_errors: Using an incorrect formula for damping coefficient β.
Confusing damping constant b with coefficient per unit mass.
Failing to relate Q to resonance sharpness.

top_down_rules.title: Verify rotational kinematic equation consistency
top_down_rules.description: Ensure that the rotational kinematic equations (e.g., θ = ω₀t + 0.5αt², ω = ω₀ + αt) are applied correctly. These equations require constant angular acceleration.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the problem explicitly states or implies constant angular acceleration. If angular acceleration is variable or unspecified, rotational kinematic equations cannot be used.
common_errors: Using rotational kinematic equations when angular acceleration is not constant.
Incorrect substitution of angular acceleration (α) or initial angular velocity (ω₀).
Mixing up linear and rotational variables (e.g., using linear acceleration in place of angular acceleration).

top_down_rules.title: Ensure consistent sign conventions for angular quantities
top_down_rules.description: Angular displacement, velocity, and acceleration can be positive or negative depending on the chosen coordinate system. Ensure consistency in the sign conventions throughout the solution.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the student has explicitly chosen a direction (e.g., counterclockwise as positive) and maintained this convention for all angular quantities. Ensure that any changes in sign are justified by the problem's setup.
common_errors: Switching sign conventions partway through the solution.
Incorrectly assigning signs to angular quantities based on direction.
Confusing clockwise and counterclockwise directions in the coordinate system.

top_down_rules.title: Validate torque equation application
top_down_rules.description: Torque (τ) is given by τ = r × F = rFsin(θ), where r is the lever arm, F is the force, and θ is the angle between r and F. This equation is valid for rigid bodies with forces applied at a fixed distance.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the student calculates torque using the correct r, F, and θ, and ensures the force is not passing through the axis of rotation. Confirm that the direction of torque is consistent with the right-hand rule.
common_errors: Forgetting to include the sin(θ) factor when torque is not perpendicular to the lever arm.
Using the wrong value for r (e.g., distance to the wrong axis of rotation).
Omitting torque contributions when multiple forces act on the body.

top_down_rules.title: Check conservation of rotational mechanical energy
top_down_rules.description: The total rotational mechanical energy (K_rot = 0.5Iω²) is conserved in the absence of non-conservative torques, such as friction. Ensure this principle is applied only when valid.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that no non-conservative torques are present before applying rotational energy conservation. If friction or other dissipative forces exist, include their work in the energy balance. Ensure that all forms of energy (rotational, translational, potential) are accounted for.
common_errors: Applying conservation of rotational energy in the presence of non-conservative torques.
Forgetting to include rotational kinetic energy in total energy calculations.
Incorrectly calculating the rotational inertia (I) of the object.

top_down_rules.title: Verify correct calculation of moment of inertia
top_down_rules.description: Moment of inertia (I) depends on the mass distribution relative to the axis of rotation. Using the correct formula or integral is critical.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the student uses the appropriate formula for I based on the geometry and axis of rotation (e.g., I = 0.5MR² for a solid disk about its central axis). For irregular objects, verify the use of integration. Ensure the parallel axis theorem is applied when the axis of rotation is shifted.
common_errors: Using the wrong formula for the shape and axis of rotation.
Forgetting to apply the parallel axis theorem when necessary.
Incorrectly calculating or integrating for non-standard geometries.

top_down_rules.title: Validate conservation of angular momentum
top_down_rules.description: Angular momentum (L = Iω) is conserved in a system with no external torques. Ensure this principle is applied only when external torques are absent.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the problem specifies or implies no external torques before assuming conservation of angular momentum. Confirm that changes in angular momentum are consistent with changes in I or ω when mass distribution changes.
common_errors: Applying conservation of angular momentum in the presence of external torques.
Incorrectly calculating angular momentum (e.g., using the wrong I or ω).
Failing to account for changes in I when the distribution of mass changes.

top_down_rules.title: Ensure correct linkage between linear and rotational kinematics
top_down_rules.description: For rolling objects or systems combining linear and rotational motion, ensure correct use of the relation v = ωr, a_t = αr, and s = θr.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the student uses the correct relationship between linear and angular quantities based on the rolling condition or constraint. Verify that rolling without slipping is explicitly stated or implied before using these relations.
common_errors: Using v = ωr when the object is not rolling without slipping.
Confusing tangential and radial acceleration.
Forgetting to apply rolling constraints when required.

top_down_rules.title: Verify dimensional and unit consistency in rotational quantities
top_down_rules.description: Ensure that all equations involving angular quantities (e.g., torque, angular momentum) are dimensionally consistent and use appropriate units (e.g., radians, N·m).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that units for angular displacement (radians), angular velocity (rad/s), angular acceleration (rad/s²), torque (N·m), and moment of inertia (kg·m²) are consistent throughout the solution. Ensure radians are used in calculations involving angular quantities.
common_errors: Using degrees instead of radians in rotational equations.
Mixing linear and angular units (e.g., using m/s instead of rad/s).
Incorrectly simplifying or canceling units in torque or energy calculations.

top_down_rules.title: Verify understanding of gyroscopic precession
top_down_rules.description: For rotating objects experiencing a torque perpendicular to their angular momentum, ensure the precession motion is correctly analyzed.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the student uses the relation Ω = τ / L, where Ω is the precession angular velocity, τ is the applied torque, and L is the angular momentum. Verify that the direction of precession is consistent with the right-hand rule.
common_errors: Incorrectly calculating the precession angular velocity.
Ignoring the direction of precession determined by the torque and angular momentum.
Confusing precession with simple rotational motion.

top_down_rules.title: Verify torque equilibrium condition
top_down_rules.description: For a system in static equilibrium, the sum of all torques acting on the system about any axis must be zero. This ensures rotational equilibrium.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the sum of torques (A3A4) equals zero around the chosen axis of rotation.
common_errors: Forgetting to include all torque contributions (e.g., reaction forces or weights)
Incorrectly calculating the lever arm (distance perpendicular to the force)
Using inconsistent torque directions (e.g., mixing clockwise and counterclockwise signs)

top_down_rules.title: Verify force equilibrium condition
top_down_rules.description: For a system in static equilibrium, the sum of all forces acting on the system in each direction (x, y, z) must be zero. This ensures translational equilibrium.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that A3A2F_x = 0, A3A2F_y = 0, and A3A2F_z = 0 for the system.
common_errors: Omitting a force component (e.g., friction or normal force)
Incorrectly resolving forces into their components
Using the wrong sign convention when summing forces

top_down_rules.title: Ensure consistent torque sign convention
top_down_rules.description: Torque direction follows a sign convention: counterclockwise torques are often considered positive, and clockwise torques are negative. This must be consistent throughout the solution.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that all torques adhere to a consistent sign convention (e.g., CCW positive, CW negative).
common_errors: Mixing clockwise and counterclockwise signs inconsistently
Using the wrong sign convention for a specific torque

top_down_rules.title: Check pivot point selection for torque analysis
top_down_rules.description: The choice of pivot point for torque calculation can be flexible, but a strategically chosen pivot point can simplify the analysis by eliminating torque contributions from unknown forces.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure the pivot point is logically selected to simplify calculations and check that torque calculations are correctly performed about this point.
common_errors: Choosing a pivot point that adds complexity unnecessarily
Omitting torque contributions about the chosen pivot point
Incorrectly assuming torque cancels at the pivot point without verification

top_down_rules.title: Ensure conditions for static equilibrium are met
top_down_rules.description: Static equilibrium assumes the system is stationary, with no net acceleration or angular acceleration. This is valid only if the system is truly at rest or moving at constant velocity.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Confirm that the system is either stationary or moving at a constant velocity before proceeding with static equilibrium equations.
common_errors: Using static equilibrium equations for a system undergoing acceleration
Neglecting external influences that could induce motion

top_down_rules.title: Verify dimensional consistency in torque calculations
top_down_rules.description: Torque is represented as the product of force in Newtons and distance in meters, thus its unit is Newton-meters (N�b7m).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure torque calculations maintain dimensional consistency with results expressed in N�b7m.
common_errors: Mixing incompatible units in torque calculations (e.g., using kilograms instead of Newtons)
Failing to multiply the force by the lever arm distance to calculate torque

top_down_rules.title: Verify geometric constraints in lever arms
top_down_rules.description: The lever arm is the shortest (perpendicular) distance from the axis of rotation to the force's line of action. Errors in geometry can skew torque calculations.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that lever arms are correctly measured as perpendicular distances to the force's line of action.
common_errors: Using an incorrect measurement for the lever arm (not perpendicular)
Misidentifying the point of application for force leading to incorrect lever arm calculations

top_down_rules.title: Ensure correct application of static friction limits
top_down_rules.description: Static friction opposes motion up to a maximum value given by f_s �A4 �B5_s�B7N, where �B5_s is the coefficient of static friction and N is the normal force.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that static friction remains within its limit �A4 �B5_s�B7N and effectively prevents motion.
common_errors: Exceeding the static friction limit in calculations
Incorrect normal force determination affecting friction calculations
Assuming static friction acts when unnecessary

top_down_rules.title: Check the angle of torque application
top_down_rules.description: Torque is maximized when force is applied perpendicular to the lever arm. The angle at which force is applied influences the torque produced.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure forces contributing to torque are evaluated considering the angle of application and its effect on torque magnitude.
common_errors: Ignoring the angle between force and lever arm
Misusing trigonometric functions to resolve torque components

experience_rules.topic: Torque and Static Equilibrium
experience_rules.title: 柔性体接触力矩建模
experience_rules.trigger: 软链/绳索在曲面上滑动并涉及刚体平衡/倾覆
experience_rules.check_logic: 必须通过积分计算接触面法向压力 $dN$ 对支点的累积力矩，而非仅使用链条重心的静力矩。

experience_rules.topic: Torque and Static Equilibrium
experience_rules.title: 刚体倾覆临界判定
experience_rules.trigger: 物体受侧向力或非对称分布载荷请求倾覆条件
experience_rules.check_logic: 检查是否以支点为轴，对比促使倾覆的力矩（如法向力、摩擦力）与阻碍倾覆的力矩（重力矩）。

topics.topic: Work-Energy Theorem and Conservation of Energy

top_down_rules.title: Verify correct application of the Work-Energy Theorem
top_down_rules.description: The Work-Energy Theorem states that the net work done on an object is equal to its change in kinetic energy (W_net = ΔKE). This applies to systems where forces are acting on a single object or a system of objects, without additional constraints like relativity or quantum effects.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the net work (sum of work done by all forces) equals the difference in kinetic energy of the object or system (KE_final - KE_initial).
common_errors: Incorrect computation of work done by individual forces.
Omission of one or more forces contributing to the net work.
Incorrect calculation of change in kinetic energy (e.g., missing 1/2 factor or squaring velocity incorrectly).

top_down_rules.title: Ensure proper use of the Conservation of Mechanical Energy
top_down_rules.description: The principle of mechanical energy conservation states that the total mechanical energy (kinetic + potential) of a system remains constant if only conservative forces (e.g., gravity, spring forces) act on it. Non-conservative forces, such as friction or air resistance, invalidate this principle.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that E_initial = E_final (KE_initial + PE_initial = KE_final + PE_final) when no non-conservative forces are present.
common_errors: Neglecting potential energy contributions for gravity or springs.
Assuming mechanical energy conservation when non-conservative forces are doing work.
Arithmetical errors in summing kinetic and potential energies.

top_down_rules.title: Account for work done by non-conservative forces
top_down_rules.description: When non-conservative forces (e.g., friction, air resistance) do work, the total mechanical energy changes. The work done by these forces is equal to the change in mechanical energy of the system (W_nc = ΔE_mechanical).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that W_nc = (KE_final + PE_final) - (KE_initial + PE_initial), where W_nc includes work from non-conservative forces.
common_errors: Omitting the contribution of non-conservative forces.
Misinterpreting the direction and sign of work done by non-conservative forces.
Assuming conservation of mechanical energy despite non-conservative forces.

top_down_rules.title: Verify correct use of sign conventions for work and energy
top_down_rules.description: Work and energy are scalar quantities but can have positive or negative signs based on the direction of forces and displacement. Work is positive if the force component is in the direction of displacement, and negative if it opposes displacement.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Confirm that work done by forces is calculated with correct attention to the angle between force and displacement. Check the sign of gravitational potential energy based on the chosen reference point.
common_errors: Incorrect sign for work done by opposing forces (e.g., friction).
Misinterpreting the angle between force and displacement.
Incorrect sign for potential energy due to inconsistent reference height.

top_down_rules.title: Check dimensional and unit consistency in work-energy calculations
top_down_rules.description: All terms in energy and work calculations should have consistent dimensions of energy (ML^2/T^2) and be expressed in compatible units (e.g., Joules in SI units).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that work, kinetic energy, and potential energy terms have consistent dimensions and units throughout the solution.
common_errors: Using incompatible units for mass, distance, and force (e.g., mixing grams with meters and Newtons).
Forgetting to square velocity in kinetic energy calculations.
Incorrect unit conversions (e.g., from cm to meters).

top_down_rules.title: Ensure applicability of conservation laws
top_down_rules.description: The Conservation of Energy principle or the Work-Energy Theorem applies only in classical mechanics for non-relativistic speeds and non-quantum scenarios. Mechanical energy conservation requires the absence of non-conservative forces.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check that the problem context does not involve relativistic speeds, quantum effects, or significant non-conservative forces when applying conservation laws.
common_errors: Applying conservation laws in scenarios with non-conservative forces without accounting for their work.
Using conservation of energy in relativistic or quantum contexts without modifications.

top_down_rules.title: Ensure geometric constraints are respected in energy calculations
top_down_rules.description: In problems involving inclined planes, pendulums, or other geometrically constrained systems, the potential energy and displacements must reflect the actual geometry of the system.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that potential energy is calculated based on the correct height, and that work calculations properly account for the displacement along the surface or path.
common_errors: Using vertical height instead of displacement along an incline.
Ignoring the geometry when calculating work done by forces.
Misrepresenting angles or distances in trigonometric calculations.

top_down_rules.title: Verify work-power relationship in dynamic systems
top_down_rules.description: Power is the rate at which work is done, and it is related to force and velocity in dynamic systems (P = F·v for constant force and velocity).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that power calculations appropriately relate to the work done over time or force applied at a specific velocity.
common_errors: Using incorrect formulas for power in dynamic systems.
Confusing instantaneous power with average power.
Neglecting time dependence when calculating work and power.

experience_rules.topic: Work-Energy Theorem and Conservation of Energy
experience_rules.title: 变力做功符号一致性检查
experience_rules.trigger: 物体在指向原点的引力/恢复力作用下向原点运动（x 减小）
experience_rules.check_logic: 检查积分表达式 ∫F dx，若力 F 与位移 dx 同向，动能增量 ΔEk 必须为正。若出现 v^2 < 0，必为积分限或力元符号错误。

symbolic_hint.canonical: W = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} F(x) dx > 0 \text{ if } sign(F) = sign(dx)

experience_rules.topic: Work-Energy Theorem and Conservation of Energy
experience_rules.title: 分段场势能连续性准则
experience_rules.trigger: 题目给出分段定义的力函数 F(x) 并要求使用能量守恒
experience_rules.check_logic: 必须通过积分定义势能 U(x) = -∫F dx，并强制要求 U(a-) = U(a+) 以确保能量在分界点连续，不可直接套用单一段的势能公式。

top_down_rules.title: Verify Band Gap Energy Calculation
top_down_rules.description: In semiconductors, the band gap energy is the energy difference between the conduction band and the valence band. This is typically used to determine the properties of semiconductor materials.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the band gap energy (Eg) is calculated using Eg = Ec - Ev, where Ec is the conduction band minimum energy and Ev is the valence band maximum energy. Additionally, verify that temperature dependence is considered if specified, as Eg can vary with temperature.
common_errors: Incorrectly identifying Ec and Ev values
Ignoring temperature dependence on Eg
Incorrect unit conversion

top_down_rules.title: Check Necessity for Population Inversion in Lasers
top_down_rules.description: Population inversion is a condition where the number of atoms in an excited state exceeds those in a lower energy state, necessary for stimulated emission in laser operation.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that N2 > N1, where N2 is the population of the upper energy state and N1 is the population of the lower energy state. Ensure that external pumping mechanisms are analyzed to confirm their adequacy in achieving population inversion.
common_errors: Confusing population inversion condition
Ignoring external pumping requirement
Misalignment of energy levels leading to incorrect states

top_down_rules.title: Validate Effective Mass Calculation
top_down_rules.description: Effective mass accounts for the influence of the periodic potential of a crystal lattice on charge carriers, affecting their acceleration in response to applied forces.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check that the effective mass m* is calculated using the curvature of the E-k (energy-momentum) relationship: m* = ħ² / (d²E/dk²). Ensure that the correct band structure model is used, and anisotropic effects are considered if applicable.
common_errors: Using incorrect band structure model
Errors in deriving second derivative
Ignoring anisotropic effects

top_down_rules.title: Verify Quantum Well Energy States Calculation
top_down_rules.description: Quantum wells confine particles to specific energy states, requiring calculations based on confinement potential and particle mass.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that energies of confined states are calculated using E_n = (n²π²ħ²)/(2m*L²), where L is well width and m* is effective mass. Verify that potential barrier effects are included in the calculation, and ensure accurate estimation of effective mass.
common_errors: Misplacing quantization of energy values
Neglecting potential barrier effects
Inaccurate estimation of effective mass

top_down_rules.title: Assess Validity of Chemical Pumping in Lasers
top_down_rules.description: Chemical reactions can be used to supply energy necessary to achieve population inversion in certain types of lasers.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that chemical pumping provides adequate energy to transition particles to higher states, facilitating population inversion. Ensure that the rate equations governing the chemical reaction are consistent with the energy requirements for the laser operation.
common_errors: Insufficient analysis of the chemical reaction contributions
Overlooking rate equations
Incorrect assumptions of energy input

top_down_rules.title: Photon Energy Conservation in Semiconductor Processes
top_down_rules.description: Energy conservation must hold during photon interactions with semiconductor materials, impacting optical properties.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check that initial photon energy equals the sum of emitted photon energy and any kinetic or thermal energy imparted to the electron. Ensure that non-radiative transitions and phonon interactions are accounted for in the energy balance.
common_errors: Neglecting absorbed energy in non-radiative transitions
Failure to account for phonon interactions
Incorrectly applying conservation to composite interactions

top_down_rules.title: Semiconductor Units Consistency Verification
top_down_rules.description: All equations used in semiconductor physics should maintain dimensional consistency and appropriate unit conversion.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure all terms in equations use consistent units (e.g., energy in electron volts [eV], charge in coulombs [C], distances in nanometers [nm]). Perform dimensional analysis to verify consistency.
common_errors: Mixing units without conversion
Ignoring dimensional analysis
Incorrect application of constants

top_down_rules.title: Validate Doping Concentration Effects in Semiconductors
top_down_rules.description: Doping concentration affects the carrier density and electrical properties of semiconductors.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that doping concentration is correctly incorporated into calculations of carrier density using n = N_d - N_a for n-type and p = N_a - N_d for p-type semiconductors, where N_d and N_a are donor and acceptor concentrations, respectively.
common_errors: Incorrect calculation of carrier density
Ignoring compensation effects in heavily doped semiconductors
Failure to account for temperature dependence of ionization

top_down_rules.title: Verify Laser Threshold Gain Condition
top_down_rules.description: The threshold gain is the minimum gain required to overcome losses in the laser cavity and achieve lasing.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the threshold gain condition is calculated using g_th = α + 1/L ln(1/R1R2), where α is the loss coefficient, L is the cavity length, and R1 and R2 are the reflectivities of the mirrors.
common_errors: Incorrect estimation of loss coefficient
Ignoring mirror reflectivity contributions
Failure to account for cavity length variations

top_down_rules.title: Verify Bohr Energy Level Quantization
top_down_rules.description: In the Bohr model, the energy levels of an electron in a hydrogen atom are quantized according to E_n = -13.6 eV/n^2, where n is the principal quantum number.
