top_down_rules.description: In Compton scattering, total energy is conserved. Ensure that the sum of the incident photon energy and the target electron's initial energy equals the sum of the scattered photon energy and the recoiling electron's energy.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check that E_photon_initial + E_electron_initial = E_photon_scattered + E_electron_recoil. Ensure the electron's initial rest energy (m_e * c^2) is included in E_electron_initial.
common_errors: Neglecting the electron's initial rest energy.
Incorrectly calculating the scattered photon's energy.
Using inconsistent units for energy terms.
Ignoring relativistic effects for high-energy photons.

top_down_rules.title: Verify momentum conservation in Compton scattering
top_down_rules.description: Momentum is conserved in Compton scattering. Ensure that the vector sum of the initial momenta equals the vector sum of the final momenta of the photon and the electron.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that p_photon_initial + p_electron_initial = p_photon_scattered + p_electron_recoil, ensuring vector components are resolved correctly. Include relativistic momentum for the electron if necessary.
common_errors: Forgetting to account for the vector nature of momentum.
Incorrectly resolving momentum components into x and y directions.
Using the wrong expressions for photon or electron momentum.
Neglecting relativistic momentum for high-energy interactions.

top_down_rules.title: Validate Compton wavelength shift formula
top_down_rules.description: Ensure the formula for Compton wavelength shift, Δλ = (h/mc)(1 - cosθ), is correctly applied, where θ is the scattering angle, h is Planck's constant, m is the electron mass, and c is the speed of light.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check that Δλ is calculated as (h/mc)(1 - cosθ), ensuring θ is in radians. Verify that h, m, and c are in consistent units.
common_errors: Using θ in degrees instead of radians.
Misplacing the factor (h/mc).
Incorrect evaluation of (1 - cosθ).
Using inconsistent units for h, m, or c.

top_down_rules.title: Ensure unit consistency for photoelectric equations
top_down_rules.description: Verify that the units in the photoelectric equation K_max = hf - ϕ are consistent, particularly ensuring energy terms are in joules or electron volts.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check that Planck's constant (h) and frequency (f) produce energy in joules, and the work function (ϕ) is in the same unit as the kinetic energy (K_max). Ensure proper conversion between joules and electron volts if necessary.
common_errors: Mixing units like joules and electron volts without conversion.
Using incorrect units for Planck's constant (e.g., J·s vs eV·s).
Neglecting unit conversion between ϕ and K_max.

top_down_rules.title: Check validity conditions for Compton scattering
top_down_rules.description: Compton scattering applies only to high-energy photons (e.g., X-rays or gamma rays) interacting with free or loosely bound electrons. Ensure the problem setup satisfies these conditions.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the incident photon energy is sufficiently high (e.g., > keV range), and the electron is either free or loosely bound. Ensure the photon energy is much greater than the electron's binding energy if the electron is not free.
common_errors: Applying Compton scattering to low-energy (visible light) photons.
Assuming tightly bound electrons instead of free electrons.
Ignoring the incident photon energy range requirement.

top_down_rules.title: Verify sign conventions in photoelectric equations
top_down_rules.description: Ensure correct sign conventions are used in the photoelectric equations, where energy terms are positive and subtractive terms (e.g., ϕ) are appropriately negative.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Confirm that energy terms (hf, ϕ, K_max) are positive, and their relationships respect the equation K_max = hf - ϕ. Ensure no negative kinetic energy is calculated.
common_errors: Assigning the wrong sign to the work function (ϕ).
Incorrectly using negative kinetic energy.
Flipping the direction of subtraction in K_max = hf - ϕ.

top_down_rules.title: Verify photon energy-wavelength relationship
top_down_rules.description: Ensure the relationship E = hc/λ is correctly applied, where E is the photon energy, h is Planck's constant, c is the speed of light, and λ is the wavelength.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check that E is calculated as hc/λ, ensuring λ is in meters and h and c are in consistent units. Verify proper conversion to electron volts if necessary.
common_errors: Using incorrect units for wavelength (e.g., nm instead of m) without conversion.
Misplacing the factors h or c in the formula.
Neglecting unit conversion for energy (e.g., joules to electron volts).

top_down_rules.title: Check Wavefunction Normalization
top_down_rules.description: The wavefunction must be normalized such that the integral of its absolute square over all space equals 1, representing total probability.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that ∫|Ψ(x)|² dx = 1 across all space, ensuring proper boundary conditions are included.
common_errors: Failing to normalize the wavefunction
Ignoring boundary conditions in infinite potential wells

top_down_rules.title: Verify de Broglie Wavelength Calculation
top_down_rules.description: Particles exhibit wave-like properties with a de Broglie wavelength given by λ = h/p, where h is Planck's constant and p is momentum.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure calculation of λ uses λ = h/p correctly. Check that momentum is derived from mass and velocity appropriately.
common_errors: Incorrect substitute of mass or velocity for momentum
Using frequency instead of momentum

top_down_rules.title: Apply Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle
top_down_rules.description: The principle states that ΔxΔp ≥ ħ/2, indicating limits on simultaneous precision of position and momentum measurements.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify scenarios where ΔxΔp ≥ ħ/2 is used, and ensure measurements account for inherent uncertainty.
common_errors: Misinterpreting uncertainty as error
Confusing uncertainty in measurement with uncertainty in prediction

top_down_rules.title: Verify Energy-Momentum Relation Consistency
top_down_rules.description: Consistent application of E = p²/2m for non-relativistic quantum particles to relate energy and momentum.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Confirm energy calculations use E = p²/2m appropriately, avoiding relativistic mass substitutions.
common_errors: Using relativistic mass instead of static mass
Confusing kinetic energy with total energy

top_down_rules.title: Adherence to Sign Conventions in Coordinate Systems
top_down_rules.description: Proper application of sign conventions for potential energy and wavefunction direction in chosen coordinate systems is necessary.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure differentiation between positive directions for momentum and potential in chosen coordinates and verify consistency in vector orientation.
common_errors: Using incorrect sign for potential energy
Misalignment of kinematic vectors in wave functions

top_down_rules.title: Validate Conditions for Photon Wave-Particle Duality
top_down_rules.description: Wave-particle duality for photons is evidential under conditions such as double-slit interference patterns.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure system meets criteria for interference conditions like slit separation comparable to wavelength, and that light's coherence is maintained.
common_errors: Assuming duality in classical macroscopic conditions
Ignoring slit geometry requirements

top_down_rules.title: Ensure Dimensional and Unit Consistency
top_down_rules.description: Physical quantities involved must be dimensionally consistent, ensuring equations balance respective units.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check all derived equations ensure unit consistency, particularly in the dimensions of energy, time, and action.
common_errors: Using incorrect units for wavelength, energy, or momentum
Discrepancies in derived units for modified equations

top_down_rules.title: Implement Probabilistic Interpretation of Quantum Mechanics
top_down_rules.description: The square of a wavefunction's amplitude gives the probability density; ensure interpretations abide probabilistic norms.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Examine probability calculations for adherence to Ψ*Ψ norms, ensuring correct integration bounds.
common_errors: Misinterpreting wavefunction absolute value for probability
Incorrect integration bounds for probability distribution

top_down_rules.title: Verify Time-Dependent Schrödinger Equation Application
top_down_rules.description: Ensure proper application of the time-dependent Schrödinger equation iħ∂Ψ/∂t = HΨ, where H is the Hamiltonian operator.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Validate that systems being analyzed account for the Hamiltonian and potential energy constraints.
common_errors: Ignoring potential energy variations over time
Incorrect formulation of the Hamiltonian

top_down_rules.title: Verify Schrödinger equation for potential barrier
top_down_rules.description: The Schrödinger equation governs quantum tunneling. For a particle approaching a potential barrier, the wavefunction must satisfy continuity and the time-independent Schrödinger equation: (-ħ²/2m)(d²ψ/dx²) + V(x)ψ = Eψ.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that Schrödinger's equation is applied correctly in the regions of the potential barrier (both inside and outside). Verify that the second derivative, potential energy, and total energy terms are correctly substituted and consistent with the problem setup.
common_errors: Neglecting the second derivative of the wavefunction
Using incorrect expressions for kinetic or potential energy terms
Misidentification of the region where V(x) applies

top_down_rules.title: Ensure wavefunction continuity at barrier boundaries
top_down_rules.description: The wavefunction ψ(x) and its first derivative dψ/dx must be continuous at the boundaries of the potential barrier for quantum tunneling to occur.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that ψ(x) and its derivative are equal on both sides of the barrier at the boundary points. Explicitly check the mathematical expressions for continuity.
common_errors: Ignoring the continuity condition for ψ(x)
Incorrect matching of derivatives at the boundary
Failing to evaluate boundary conditions explicitly

top_down_rules.title: Check for conservation of probability current
top_down_rules.description: The probability current (J) must be conserved throughout the tunneling process. For a one-dimensional case, J = (ħ/2mi) [ψ*(dψ/dx) - (dψ*/dx)ψ].
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the probability current is the same on both sides of the potential barrier. Verify the calculation of J explicitly and check for sign consistency.
common_errors: Not calculating probability current at all
Incorrect signs in the probability current formula
Assuming probability current is zero on one side

top_down_rules.title: Verify calculation for tunneling probability
top_down_rules.description: The tunneling probability (T) is given by T = exp(-2κa), where κ = sqrt(2m(V₀ - E))/ħ and a is the width of the potential barrier.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the exponent in the tunneling probability formula is correctly calculated, using proper values for κ and a. Verify that all constants and units are consistent.
common_errors: Using incorrect units for barrier width or energy
Neglecting the negative sign in the exponent
Incorrect calculation of κ (e.g., forgetting ħ or using wrong mass)

top_down_rules.title: Verify sign conventions for potential energies
top_down_rules.description: When assigning the potential energy V(x), ensure that the barrier height V₀ and the particle's energy E are correctly differentiated, with V(x) > E in the barrier region for tunneling.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Confirm that V(x) > E in the barrier region and that the particle's energy is less than the barrier height. Verify that the sign conventions are consistent throughout the problem.
common_errors: Reversing the inequality between V(x) and E
Assigning incorrect potential values to regions outside the barrier
Using arbitrary sign conventions without justification

top_down_rules.title: Confirm potential barrier geometry constraints
top_down_rules.description: Quantum tunneling assumes a well-defined potential barrier of finite height and width. The geometry of the barrier (e.g., rectangular) must be explicitly stated or derived.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check that the potential barrier's height (V₀) and width (a) are finite and defined in the problem description. Ensure that the geometry is consistent with the tunneling scenario.
common_errors: Assuming an infinitely high or wide barrier without justification
Using inconsistent or undefined barrier parameters
Failing to specify the barrier geometry

top_down_rules.title: Verify dimensional consistency in tunneling equations
top_down_rules.description: Ensure that all terms in the Schrödinger equation and derived formulas for tunneling probability, wavefunction, and energy have consistent dimensions.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that ħ²/2m has dimensions of energy, κ has dimensions of inverse length, and T is dimensionless. Check that all units are consistent throughout the calculations.
common_errors: Forgetting ħ in calculations, leading to incorrect dimensions
Using inconsistent units for mass, energy, or length
Incorrect dimensional analysis of derived quantities like κ or T

top_down_rules.title: Confirm validity conditions for quantum tunneling
top_down_rules.description: Quantum tunneling applies only when the particle's energy (E) is less than the barrier height (V₀). Additionally, the system must be quantum-mechanical (small-scale, typically atomic-level phenomena).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that E < V₀ and that the problem context justifies the application of quantum mechanics. Verify that the scale of the system is appropriate for quantum effects.
common_errors: Applying tunneling to classical-scale systems
Assuming tunneling occurs when E > V₀
Ignoring the quantum nature of the problem

top_down_rules.title: Verify wavefunction normalization
top_down_rules.description: The wavefunction must be normalized such that the total probability of finding the particle is 1. This ensures physical consistency.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the integral of |ψ(x)|² over all space equals 1. Check for proper normalization constants in the wavefunction.
common_errors: Failing to normalize the wavefunction
Using incorrect normalization constants
Ignoring the normalization condition entirely

top_down_rules.title: Verify the relativistic energy-momentum relation
top_down_rules.description: The fundamental equation relating energy, momentum, and mass in relativity is E² = (pc)² + (mc²)². This relation holds for all particles, whether massless or massive.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the total energy squared equals the sum of the squared momentum term (pc)² and the squared rest energy term (mc²)².
common_errors: Incorrect computation of total energy (E).
Omitting the momentum term for moving particles.
Forgetting to square terms in the energy-momentum equation.

top_down_rules.title: Verify rest energy calculation
top_down_rules.description: Rest energy is given by the equation E_rest = mc², where m is the rest mass of the particle. This applies only when the particle is at rest (momentum p = 0).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if rest energy is calculated as mc² when the particle is at rest (p = 0).
common_errors: Confusing rest mass with relativistic mass.
Using velocity-dependent mass for rest energy calculation.
Incorrectly adding momentum contributions to rest energy.

top_down_rules.title: Check energy-momentum consistency for massless particles
top_down_rules.description: For massless particles (e.g., photons), the energy E and momentum p are related by E = pc. The rest mass term (mc²) drops out in this case.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that for massless particles, E = pc is used, and rest energy is not included.
common_errors: Including rest energy for massless particles.
Using incorrect formulas for energy-momentum relation.
Mixing up units of energy and momentum.

top_down_rules.title: Ensure correct sign conventions for momentum and energy
top_down_rules.description: Relativistic momentum is a vector quantity, and its sign depends on the coordinate system used. Energy is always positive, as it represents a scalar quantity.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that energy is non-negative and that momentum's direction is consistent with the chosen coordinate system.
common_errors: Assigning negative energy values.
Inconsistent sign conventions for momentum components.
Misinterpreting direction of momentum vectors.

top_down_rules.title: Check velocity constraints for relativistic equations
top_down_rules.description: The velocity of any particle in relativistic mechanics must always be less than the speed of light (v < c). This is a fundamental constraint of special relativity.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that any velocity used in relativistic equations satisfies the condition v < c.
common_errors: Using velocities greater than or equal to the speed of light.
Confusing relativistic velocities with classical limits.
Incorrect unit conversions leading to v >= c.

top_down_rules.title: Verify dimensional consistency of relativistic equations
top_down_rules.description: All terms in relativistic equations must have consistent dimensions. For example, energy terms should have units of joules or equivalent, and momentum terms should have units of kg·m/s.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if all terms in the equations have consistent units and dimensions, specifically [E] = joules and [p] = kg·m/s.
common_errors: Mixing units of energy and momentum.
Incorrect conversions between mass, momentum, and energy terms.
Omitting factors of c in relativistic equations.

top_down_rules.title: Verify calculation of relativistic kinetic energy
top_down_rules.description: The relativistic kinetic energy is given by KE = (γ - 1)mc², where γ = 1 / √(1 - v²/c²). This applies to particles with v > 0.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that relativistic kinetic energy is calculated using KE = (γ - 1)mc² and that γ is computed correctly.
common_errors: Using classical kinetic energy formula (1/2mv²) instead of relativistic formula.
Incorrect computation of γ factor.
Forgetting to subtract the rest energy term from total energy to calculate KE.

top_down_rules.title: Check conservation of relativistic energy and momentum
top_down_rules.description: In any relativistic system, the total energy and momentum must be conserved. This applies to closed systems undergoing collisions or interactions.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the total energy and momentum before and after an interaction remain conserved.
common_errors: Omitting contributions from rest energy in total energy calculations.
Failing to account for vector nature of momentum in collisions.
Neglecting mass-energy equivalence in conservation equations.

top_down_rules.title: Verify invariant mass calculation
top_down_rules.description: Invariant mass, or rest mass, is consistent across all reference frames and is calculated using the relation E² - (pc)² = (m₀c²)².
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that invariant mass is correctly calculated and consistent across different reference frames using E² - (pc)² = (m₀c²)².
common_errors: Confusing invariant mass with relativistic mass.
Incorrectly applying the invariant mass formula in varying reference frames.

top_down_rules.title: Verify Time-Independent Schrödinger Equation Formulation
top_down_rules.description: The time-independent Schrödinger equation (TISE) for a particle in a potential V(x) is given by: -ħ²/2m * d²ψ/dx² + Vψ = Eψ. This equation describes the behavior of a quantum particle in a stationary state.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure the equation is represented as -ħ²/2m * d²ψ/dx² + Vψ - Eψ = 0 and that all terms are correctly included.
common_errors: Incorrect coefficient of second derivative term (missing or incorrect ħ²/2m factor)
Omitting potential energy term Vψ from the equation
Incorrect sign usage for the energy term

top_down_rules.title: Wavefunction Normalization Requirement
top_down_rules.description: A wavefunction representing a quantum system must be normalized such that the integral over all space of |ψ(x)|² equals 1, ensuring it represents a valid probability distribution.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if ∫ |ψ(x)|² dx = 1 over all space, and verify that normalization is explicitly applied if the wavefunction is not already normalized.
common_errors: Neglecting the normalization condition
Incorrectly evaluating the integral bounds
Normalization factor not applied or incorrect in the wavefunction

top_down_rules.title: Correct Sign Convention for Wavefunction
top_down_rules.description: Wavefunctions are complex functions, and their phase does not affect probabilities. However, consistent use of sign convention is necessary, particularly in interference contexts.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check that the sign of the imaginary unit i in exponential forms is consistent, and ensure phase differences between superposed states are handled correctly.
common_errors: Incorrect handling of complex conjugates
Missed phase factor leading to incorrect probability calculations
Sign errors in potential functions or wavefunctions

top_down_rules.title: Validation for Schrödinger Equation Applicability
top_down_rules.description: The Schrödinger equation is applicable in non-relativistic quantum mechanics. It must be used in contexts where particle speeds are well below the speed of light, such that relativistic effects are negligible.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the problem context does not involve relativistic speeds or gravitational fields affecting quantum states significantly. If relativistic effects are significant, the Dirac equation or other relativistic formulations should be used.
common_errors: Applying Schrödinger equation in relativistic scenarios
Ignoring significant external fields altering quantum dynamics
Mistaking highly relativistic contexts for non-relativistic

top_down_rules.title: Boundary Conditions for Wavefunctions
top_down_rules.description: Wavefunctions must satisfy specific boundary conditions depending on the physical problem, such as ψ(x) = 0 at potential barriers or infinity for bound states.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check whether the wavefunction adheres to required boundary conditions (e.g., ψ(x) approaches zero at infinity for bound states) and ensure continuity of ψ(x) and its derivative at potential discontinuities.
common_errors: Incorrect application of boundary conditions
Overlooking boundary conditions at discontinuities
Ignoring behavior at potential barriers

top_down_rules.title: Dimensional Consistency in Schrödinger Equation
top_down_rules.description: Ensure all terms in the Schrödinger equation are dimensionally consistent. The kinetic energy term -ħ²/2m * d²ψ/dx² must have dimensions of energy.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify each term in the equation has the dimension of energy, typically [ML²T⁻²] in SI units, and confirm that Planck's constant ħ and mass m are used with correct units.
common_errors: Mismatched units within Schrödinger equation terms
Incorrect handling of units for Planck's constant ħ
Errors in unit conversion affecting the equation consistency

top_down_rules.title: Correct Calculation of Probability Current Density
top_down_rules.description: For a wavefunction ψ(x,t), the probability current density j(x,t) is given as j = (ħ/m)*Im(ψ*∇ψ), which relates the flow of probability in space.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that probability current density is calculated with proper use of complex conjugates, the imaginary component extraction, and correct application of ħ/m.
common_errors: Mistakes in complex conjugate calculation
Not factoring ħ/m correctly
Neglecting processes for extracting the imaginary part

top_down_rules.title: Wavefunction Continuity at Potential Discontinuities
top_down_rules.description: Wavefunctions and their first derivatives must be continuous at potential discontinuities, ensuring physical consistency.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that ψ(x) and dψ/dx are continuous across potential discontinuities, except in cases of infinite potential barriers where ψ(x) = 0.
common_errors: Discontinuity in ψ(x) at finite potential steps
Incorrect handling of derivative continuity
Misinterpreting infinite potential barriers

top_down_rules.title: Verify correctness of time dilation equation usage
top_down_rules.description: The time dilation formula is t' = t / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2), where t is the proper time, v is the relative velocity, and c is the speed of light. It applies when measuring time intervals for an event in two different inertial frames.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the equation t' = t / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) is used correctly. Verify that t is the proper time (measured in the rest frame of the event), v is the relative velocity between the frames, and c is the speed of light. Ensure all variables are substituted with physically valid values.
common_errors: Forgetting to square the velocity (v^2/c^2).
Using addition instead of subtraction in the Lorentz factor denominator.
Incorrectly identifying t as the proper time instead of the observer's time.

top_down_rules.title: Verify application of length contraction equation
top_down_rules.description: The length contraction formula is L' = L * sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2), where L is the proper length (length measured at rest) and L' is the contracted length observed from a moving frame. It applies only for objects moving parallel to their length.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the equation L' = L * sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) is applied correctly. Verify that L is the proper length, v is the relative velocity parallel to the object's length, and c is the speed of light. Ensure the situation involves motion parallel to the object's length.
common_errors: Forgetting to square the velocity term in v^2/c^2.
Using the formula for objects not aligned with the direction of motion.
Switching L and L' in the equation.

top_down_rules.title: Enforce the constraint that v < c
top_down_rules.description: In special relativity, the relative velocity v between two inertial frames must be less than the speed of light (c). This is a fundamental constraint of the theory.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that any relative velocity used in calculations satisfies v < c. Verify that v is a positive, real number and does not exceed the speed of light.
common_errors: Using a relative velocity v >= c.
Substituting an unphysical value for v (e.g., negative or imaginary velocities).

top_down_rules.title: Verify dimensional consistency of Lorentz factor
top_down_rules.description: The Lorentz factor, gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2), must be dimensionless since it represents a scaling factor. This ensures that all quantities derived using it are dimensionally consistent.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check that v and c are in the same units (e.g., both in m/s) before evaluating the Lorentz factor. Confirm that the resulting Lorentz factor is dimensionless.
common_errors: Using mismatched units for v and c (e.g., m/s vs km/s).
Failing to confirm that the Lorentz factor is dimensionless.

top_down_rules.title: Ensure consistent use of inertial frames and coordinate systems
top_down_rules.description: Special relativity requires the use of inertial reference frames (non-accelerating). Calculations involving time dilation and length contraction must be performed within such frames.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the problem explicitly involves inertial frames and that no accelerations are introduced in the setup. Ensure the proper frame is correctly identified (e.g., rest frame vs moving frame).
common_errors: Applying special relativity equations in scenarios with accelerating frames.
Misidentifying which frame is the proper frame (e.g., confusing the moving frame with the rest frame).

top_down_rules.title: Verify that relativity of simultaneity is considered
top_down_rules.description: In special relativity, events that are simultaneous in one frame may not be simultaneous in another. Ensure this principle is accounted for in multi-event problems.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check whether the problem examines how simultaneity is affected when switching between reference frames. Verify that time coordinates are transformed appropriately for different frames.
common_errors: Assuming absolute simultaneity across frames.
Failing to transform time coordinates appropriately for different frames.

top_down_rules.title: Confirm conditions for applying special relativity
top_down_rules.description: Special relativity applies only to inertial frames in flat spacetime. It does not apply in regions with significant gravitational fields or accelerating reference frames.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure the problem setup explicitly states or implies flat spacetime and inertial frames. Verify that no gravitational effects or accelerations are present in the scenario.
common_errors: Applying special relativity in scenarios involving gravity without transitioning to general relativity.
Using special relativity equations in non-inertial (accelerating) frames.

top_down_rules.title: Ensure unit consistency in relativistic calculations
top_down_rules.description: All quantities (time, length, velocity, etc.) must be in consistent units (e.g., SI units) when performing calculations in special relativity.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check that units are consistent for time, length, and velocity in all equations. Ensure the speed of light (c) is used in consistent units. Verify that no unit mismatches occur during calculations.
common_errors: Using inconsistent units for v and c (e.g., m/s for v and km/s for c).
Mixing time units (e.g., seconds for t and hours for t').

top_down_rules.title: Verify causality is preserved
top_down_rules.description: Special relativity enforces causality, meaning no information or influence can travel faster than the speed of light. This ensures that cause precedes effect in all reference frames.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that no scenario involves information or objects traveling faster than the speed of light. Verify that time ordering of causally connected events is preserved across all frames.
common_errors: Allowing superluminal (faster-than-light) information transfer.
Misinterpreting time ordering of causally connected events.

top_down_rules.title: Calculate magnetic moment using μ = I·A
top_down_rules.description: The magnetic moment (μ) of a current-carrying loop is given by μ = I·A, where I is the current and A is the area vector of the loop. The direction of μ is determined by the right-hand rule.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify if μ = I·A is used, with A as the area of the loop and its direction calculated using the right-hand rule. Ensure the current (I) and area (A) are correctly measured and substituted.
common_errors: Incorrect calculation of the loop area A.
Forgetting to use the right-hand rule for direction.
Using incorrect units for current (I) or area.

top_down_rules.title: Ensure spin quantization is applied (±ħ/2 for fermions)
top_down_rules.description: Spin is quantized, and for fermions like electrons, the spin can only take values of ±ħ/2. For bosons, it can take integer multiples of ħ.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that spin values are quantized as ±ħ/2 for fermions or integer multiples of ħ for bosons. Ensure the particle type (fermion or boson) is correctly identified.
common_errors: Assigning non-quantized spin values.
Mixing fermion and boson spin characteristics.
Confusing spin angular momentum with orbital angular momentum.

top_down_rules.title: Use correct gyromagnetic ratio for spin magnetic moment
top_down_rules.description: The spin magnetic moment μ_s of a particle is related to its spin S by μ_s = g·(e/2m)·S, where g is the gyromagnetic ratio, e is the charge, and m is the mass of the particle.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the gyromagnetic ratio (g) is chosen appropriately for the particle type (e.g., g ≈ 2 for electrons). Ensure the correct values for charge (e) and mass (m) are used.
common_errors: Using incorrect g-factor for the particle.
Confusing g-factor for orbital and spin magnetic moments.
Incorrect substitution of particle mass or charge.

top_down_rules.title: Verify use of the Bohr magneton for electron magnetic moment
top_down_rules.description: The Bohr magneton, μ_B = eħ/2m_e, is the unit of magnetic moment for electrons. It is frequently used in calculations involving spin and orbital magnetic moments.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the Bohr magneton formula μ_B = eħ/2m_e is applied for electron magnetic moment calculations. Ensure the correct values for e, ħ, and m_e are used.
common_errors: Using the Bohr magneton for particles other than electrons.
Omitting ħ or using an incorrect value.
Confusing the electron mass (m_e) with other masses.

top_down_rules.title: Ensure dimensional consistency of magnetic moment calculations
top_down_rules.description: The magnetic moment has SI units of A·m² (ampere square meters). All related calculations should maintain dimensional consistency.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the result of magnetic moment calculations has the correct units of A·m² and that intermediate steps are dimensionally consistent. Ensure proper unit conversions if necessary.
common_errors: Mismatch of units in area or current.
Omitting or incorrectly converting units like A or m².
Mixing CGS and SI unit systems without proper conversion.

top_down_rules.title: Apply Larmor precession correctly in external magnetic fields
top_down_rules.description: Larmor precession occurs when a magnetic moment experiences a torque in an external magnetic field. The angular frequency of precession is given by ω_L = γ·B, where γ is the gyromagnetic ratio and B is the magnetic field strength.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that ω_L = γ·B is used and that γ is correctly specified for the particle in question. Ensure the magnetic field vector B is correctly measured and accounted for.
common_errors: Using an incorrect gyromagnetic ratio γ.
Confusing the direction of precession with the direction of the magnetic field.
Forgetting to account for the vector nature of B.

top_down_rules.title: Check Pauli exclusion principle for spin states
top_down_rules.description: The Pauli exclusion principle states that no two fermions can occupy the same quantum state simultaneously. This applies to spin states in multi-electron systems.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that no two fermions in the same system are assigned identical quantum numbers, including spin. Ensure the quantum state is fully specified, including orbital and spin components.
common_errors: Assigning identical spin states to two fermions in the same orbital.
Misidentifying particles as fermions or bosons.
Neglecting spin as part of the quantum state.

top_down_rules.title: Follow correct sign convention for the magnetic moment direction
top_down_rules.description: The direction of the magnetic moment is determined by the right-hand rule relative to the current or spin angular momentum. Ensure this convention is followed consistently.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check that the magnetic moment direction aligns with the right-hand rule relative to the current or spin angular momentum. Verify that the current or spin direction is correctly identified.
common_errors: Reversing the direction of the magnetic moment.
Ignoring the right-hand rule in determining direction.
Confusing the direction of current with the direction of the magnetic field.

top_down_rules.title: Verify application of the Zeeman effect in magnetic fields
top_down_rules.description: The Zeeman effect describes the splitting of energy levels of an atom or particle in the presence of an external magnetic field. The energy shift is given by ΔE = μ·B, where μ is the magnetic moment and B is the magnetic field strength.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that ΔE = μ·B is used correctly, with μ and B properly calculated and aligned. Ensure the splitting is consistent with the particle's magnetic moment and quantum state.
common_errors: Incorrect calculation of the energy shift ΔE.
Using an incorrect magnetic moment μ.
Neglecting the vector nature of B in the calculation.

top_down_rules.title: Verify interactions adhere to the four fundamental forces
top_down_rules.description: Ensure that all interactions in the problem are described by one or more of the four fundamental forces: gravitational, electromagnetic, weak nuclear, or strong nuclear. The Standard Model does not account for gravitational interactions explicitly, so its absence in particle physics calculations is acceptable.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if any interaction is attributed to a force outside the four fundamental forces. Ensure gravitational forces are not mistakenly included in Standard Model calculations.
common_errors: Attributing particle decay processes to gravitational forces
Confusing weak nuclear force with electromagnetic force in beta decay

top_down_rules.title: Ensure conservation laws are satisfied
top_down_rules.description: In the Standard Model, the conservation of energy, momentum, angular momentum, electric charge, lepton number, and baryon number must be upheld. Violations of these conservation laws indicate an error unless explicitly stated otherwise (e.g., in certain neutrino oscillation contexts).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the total values of conserved quantities before and after an interaction, decay, or collision are equal.
common_errors: Forgetting to conserve lepton number in weak interactions
Neglecting angular momentum conservation in particle collisions
Failing to conserve baryon number in hadron decays

top_down_rules.title: Verify particle quark composition adheres to Standard Model
top_down_rules.description: Check that the quark composition of hadrons (baryons and mesons) is consistent with the Standard Model. For example, baryons must consist of three quarks, and mesons must consist of one quark and one antiquark.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure baryons have three quarks and mesons have one quark-antiquark pair. Verify that the quark types and charges sum to the particle's total charge.
common_errors: Using invalid quark combinations for baryons or mesons
Misassigning quark charges, leading to incorrect particle charge

top_down_rules.title: Validate Feynman diagram vertex rules
top_down_rules.description: Ensure that each vertex in a Feynman diagram respects the Standard Model rules. For example, vertices must conserve charge, and interactions must involve proper coupling (e.g., gluons coupling only to quarks, not leptons).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check that all vertices conserve charge and involve interactions allowed by the Standard Model (e.g., photon-electron, gluon-quark).
common_errors: Allowing gluons to couple to leptons
Neglecting charge conservation at a vertex
Drawing a vertex with incompatible particles (e.g., electron, W+, and gluon)

top_down_rules.title: Verify dimensional and unit consistency in calculations
top_down_rules.description: Ensure all terms in equations and calculations have consistent units. For example, particle masses should be in energy units (e.g., MeV/c²), and cross-sections should be in area units (e.g., barns).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check that all terms in equations have matching units. Ensure Planck's constant (h) and the speed of light (c) are appropriately included in unit conversions.
common_errors: Using mass in kilograms instead of energy units like MeV/c²
Forgetting to include c² in energy-mass equivalence calculations
Mixing unit systems (e.g., SI and natural units) inconsistently

top_down_rules.title: Ensure correct charge sign conventions
top_down_rules.description: Verify that particle charges are assigned with the correct sign and magnitude (e.g., electron: -1e, proton: +1e, up quark: +2/3e, down quark: -1/3e).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check that charges of particles match their Standard Model definitions and are consistently used in calculations.
common_errors: Assigning a positive charge to an electron
Using incorrect fractional charges for quarks
Flipping the sign of charges in Feynman diagram calculations

top_down_rules.title: Check applicability of the Standard Model
top_down_rules.description: Ensure the problem falls within the domain of the Standard Model. The Standard Model applies to electromagnetic, weak, and strong interactions but does not include gravity or phenomena explained by general relativity or quantum gravity.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Confirm that the problem involves energies, particles, and interactions within the scope of the Standard Model. Flag instances where quantum gravity or relativistic effects dominate.
common_errors: Applying Standard Model equations to black hole interactions
Using Standard Model to explain phenomena at Planck scale
Neglecting relativistic corrections when they are significant

top_down_rules.title: Detect symmetry violations
top_down_rules.description: Ensure that physical processes respect the symmetries of the Standard Model unless explicitly stated otherwise (e.g., CP-violation in certain decays). Common symmetries include charge conservation, parity conservation (where applicable), and CPT invariance.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the process violates any symmetry without justification. For example, ensure CPT symmetry is preserved in all interactions.
common_errors: Ignoring CP-violation in weak decays
Mistaking parity violation for charge violation
Neglecting CPT symmetry in particle-antiparticle calculations

topics.topic: Wave-Particle Duality and de Broglie Wavelength

top_down_rules.title: Apply de Broglie wavelength equation
top_down_rules.description: The de Broglie wavelength equation, λ = h/p, relates the wavelength of a particle to its momentum, where h is Planck's constant. It applies to all matter exhibiting wave-like properties.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify the use of λ = h/p for particles demonstrating wave-like characteristics.
common_errors: Using incorrect values for h
Mixing up momentum and velocity
Incorrect units conversion between mass, velocity, and wavelength

top_down_rules.title: Ensure dimensional consistency in de Broglie wavelength calculations
top_down_rules.description: When calculating de Broglie wavelength, ensure unit consistency by confirming that momentum p is in the proper units (kg*m/s) and wavelength λ is in meters, guaranteeing dimensionally accurate summaries like λ = h/p.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Confirm that units of momentum and wavelength conform to the SI unit system.
common_errors: Using momentum in units other than kg*m/s
Calculating wavelength in centimeters instead of meters
Mismatched units that lead to incorrect quantity calculations

top_down_rules.title: Verify conditions for applying wave-particle duality
top_down_rules.description: Wave-particle duality is most evident for microscopic particles with low mass. Ensure its application only for particles where classical mechanics are insufficient and quantum effects are significant.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Confirm application for particles where quantum mechanical effects dominate (typically microscopic entities).
common_errors: Using wave-particle duality for macroscopic objects without justification
Neglecting the applicability of classical mechanics in favor of quantum without justification

top_down_rules.title: Apply consistent sign conventions in wave motion
top_down_rules.description: When analyzing wave properties through de Broglie wavelength, ensure velocity and momentum directions are checked against chosen coordinate systems for consistency in sign conventions.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify positive and negative directions in chosen coordinate system are consistently applied to momentum and velocity when determining wavelength.
common_errors: Mixing up positive and negative directions
Incorrectly factoring direction into momentum, affecting wavelength calculation

top_down_rules.title: Check geometric constraints in wave-particle analysis
top_down_rules.description: When examining wave-particle duality, ensure geometric constraints like boundary conditions are considered to predict interference and diffraction patterns correctly.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Evaluate if boundary conditions or geometric constraints are considered to anticipate wave behaviors like diffraction.
common_errors: Ignoring boundary constraints and geometry in setups impacting wave patterns
Failing to account for source arrangement in interference scenarios

top_down_rules.title: Correlate kinetic energy with de Broglie wavelength
top_down_rules.description: Kinetic energy is linked to the de Broglie wavelength as E_k = p^2/(2m). Ensure step linkage between energy calculations and wavelength conversion.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure kinetic energy computations precede momentum determination for de Broglie wavelength calculation.
common_errors: Ignoring kinetic energy role in wavelength calculations
Confusing energy formulas leading to erroneous wavelength values

top_down_rules.title: Introduce wave-particle duality before advanced analysis
top_down_rules.description: Students must establish foundational understanding of wave-particle duality principles starting with basic experiments like the double-slit before mastering de Broglie wavelength calculations.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Validate student proficiency with fundamental wave-particle concepts as precursor to complex analytical problems.
common_errors: Prematurely diving into calculations without understanding core principles
Neglecting introductory experiments crucial for concept comprehension

top_down_rules.title: Assess the significance of quantum effects in wave-particle duality
top_down_rules.description: It is crucial to differentiate scenarios where quantum effects significantly influence particle behavior, such as in atomic scale phenomena.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Evaluate whether the significance of quantum effects is accounted for in scenarios where classical mechanics fail to describe the system accurately.
common_errors: Overlooking crucial quantum effects in small-scale interactions
Misapplying classical mechanics to systems dominated by quantum behaviors

top_down_rules.title: Verify use of paraxial approximation
top_down_rules.description: The paraxial approximation assumes that light rays make small angles with the optical axis, which simplifies the equations for aberrations. This approximation is essential for minimizing errors in calculations of spherical aberrations and other optical defects.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the angles of incidence or refraction are small enough (sin(θ) ≈ θ in radians) and whether this assumption is explicitly stated in the solution.
common_errors: Failing to verify the validity of the paraxial approximation before applying it.
Using paraxial formulas in systems with large angles of incidence.
Ignoring higher-order terms that are significant for non-paraxial rays.

top_down_rules.title: Ensure correct sign convention for lens aberrations
top_down_rules.description: Sign conventions in optical systems are crucial for determining the nature of aberrations. For example, positive focal lengths indicate converging lenses, whereas negative focal lengths indicate diverging lenses.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the sign convention (e.g., object distance, image distance, focal length) is consistent with the system being described, and ensure correct characterization of aberrations as positive or negative.
common_errors: Assigning the wrong sign to focal lengths for different lens types.
Confusing light propagation direction when determining aberrations.
Mixing sign conventions between different parts of the optical system.

top_down_rules.title: Check inclusion of spherical aberration formula
top_down_rules.description: Spherical aberration arises due to the inability of spherical lenses or mirrors to focus all incoming rays to a single point.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify if the spherical aberration formula Δx = (h^2 / 8R^3) * (n^2 - 1) is used correctly, where h is the height of the ray, R is the radius of curvature, and n is the refractive index.
common_errors: Omitting the h^2 term, which accounts for the ray height.
Incorrectly substituting the radius of curvature.
Ignoring the refractive index in the formula.

top_down_rules.title: Verify chromatic aberration calculations
top_down_rules.description: Chromatic aberration is caused by the dispersion of light, leading to different refraction for different wavelengths.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the dispersion relation Δf = f * (n_v - n_r) / (n - 1) is correctly applied, where n_v and n_r are refractive indices for violet and red light.
common_errors: Ignoring wavelength dependence in refractive indices.
Using incorrect or arbitrary values for n_v and n_r.
Failing to account for the range of light wavelengths in the system.

top_down_rules.title: Check distortion aberration types
top_down_rules.description: Distortion occurs when magnification varies across the field of view, leading to pincushion or barrel distortions.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify if the solution correctly identifies the distortion type based on magnification formula M = (image height) / (object height) and variations across the field.
common_errors: Failing to distinguish between pincushion and barrel distortions.
Incorrectly calculating magnification values at different field points.
Not addressing distortion effects in wide-angle lenses.

top_down_rules.title: Ensure unit consistency in aberration equations
top_down_rules.description: Aberration calculations require consistent usage of dimensions like lengths (meters), angles (radians), and refractive indices (dimensionless).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if all terms in aberration equations have consistent units, and confirm unit conversion where necessary.
common_errors: Using inconsistent units for focal length, radius of curvature, or distances.
Forgetting to convert angles to radians where required.
Mixing SI and non-SI units in intermediate steps.

top_down_rules.title: Verify condition for coma aberration
top_down_rules.description: Coma aberration occurs for off-axis sources resulting in comet-like images due to variation in magnification.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure coma is considered for off-axis points and verify the use of the formula Δx = (h^2 / 2f) * θ, with θ as the angle subtended by the aperture at the lens center.
common_errors: Wrongly applying coma aberration formulas for on-axis sources.
Ignoring the off-axis angle in calculations.
Identifying coma mistakenly as spherical aberration.

top_down_rules.title: Check validity of thin lens approximation
top_down_rules.description: The thin lens approximation assumes lens thickness is negligible compared to its focal length and radii of curvature.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify lens thickness is sufficiently small compared to its focal length and radii of curvature to justify the thin lens approximation.
common_errors: Using the thin lens approximation for thick lenses without justification.
Neglecting the thickness term in significant aberration calculations.
Confusing thin lens approximation with paraxial approximation.

top_down_rules.title: Verify Brewster's angle equation
top_down_rules.description: Brewster's angle is calculated using the equation tan(θ_B) = n_2 / n_1, where θ_B is the Brewster's angle, and n_1 and n_2 are the refractive indices of the two media. This equation holds for light incident at the boundary between two transparent media.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if tan(θ_B) equals the ratio of n_2 to n_1 (i.e., tan(θ_B) = n_2 / n_1). Ensure θ_B is in radians for trigonometric calculations.
common_errors: Using wrong refractive indices (e.g., swapping n_1 and n_2)
Using sin or cos instead of tan
Forgetting to convert angle to radians for trigonometric calculations

top_down_rules.title: Verify Malus's Law equation
top_down_rules.description: Malus's Law states that the transmitted intensity of polarized light through a polarizer is given by I = I_0 * cos^2(θ), where I_0 is the initial intensity and θ is the angle between the light's polarization direction and the axis of the polarizer.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the transmitted intensity I matches I_0 * cos^2(θ). Ensure θ is in radians for trigonometric calculations.
common_errors: Using sin^2 instead of cos^2
Mixing up the angle θ with other angles in the problem
Forgetting to square the cosine term
Forgetting to convert angle to radians for trigonometric calculations

top_down_rules.title: Ensure correct sign convention for Brewster's angle
top_down_rules.description: For Brewster's angle calculations, θ_B must always be positive and measured with respect to the normal of the interface.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that θ_B is positive and calculated with respect to the normal, not the surface.
common_errors: Measuring θ_B with respect to the surface instead of the normal
Using negative values for angles

top_down_rules.title: Check sign and reference for angle in Malus's Law
top_down_rules.description: The angle θ in Malus's Law must be the relative angle between the polarization direction of incident light and the transmission axis of the polarizer. Ensure this angle is correctly determined.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that θ is the relative angle between the light's polarization and the polarizer's axis, and not an absolute angle.
common_errors: Using an absolute angle instead of the relative angle
Using the complementary angle unintentionally

top_down_rules.title: Check physical constraints for Brewster's angle
top_down_rules.description: Brewster's angle is only defined when light passes from one transparent medium to another. It is not defined for opaque materials or when n_2 < 0.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that both n_1 and n_2 are positive and represent refractive indices of transparent media.
common_errors: Using negative or zero values for refractive indices
Attempting to calculate Brewster's angle between a transparent and an opaque medium

top_down_rules.title: Ensure Malus's Law applies to polarized light
top_down_rules.description: Malus's Law only applies to polarized light. If the incident light is unpolarized, Malus's Law cannot be directly applied without additional considerations.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the incident light is polarized. If unpolarized, ensure the light is converted to polarized before applying Malus's Law.
common_errors: Applying Malus's Law to unpolarized light
Forgetting to account for partial polarization

top_down_rules.title: Check dimensional consistency for Malus's Law
top_down_rules.description: The transmitted intensity I and initial intensity I_0 must have the same units, and cos^2(θ) is dimensionless.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that I and I_0 are expressed in the same units and that cos^2(θ) is dimensionless.
common_errors: Using inconsistent units for I and I_0
Incorrectly introducing dimensions into cos^2(θ)

top_down_rules.title: Check dimensional consistency for Brewster's angle
top_down_rules.description: The refractive indices n_1 and n_2 are dimensionless, and tan(θ_B) must also be dimensionless.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that n_1 and n_2 are dimensionless quantities and that tan(θ_B) is calculated correctly.
common_errors: Using refractive indices with incorrect dimensions
Introducing angles in degrees without conversion to radians for trigonometric functions

top_down_rules.title: Account for partial polarization in Malus's Law
top_down_rules.description: If the incident light is partially polarized, Malus's Law must be applied only to the polarized component of the light. The unpolarized component remains unaffected by the polarizer.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify if the incident light is partially polarized. If so, separate the polarized and unpolarized components and apply Malus's Law only to the polarized component.
common_errors: Applying Malus's Law to the entire intensity of partially polarized light
Ignoring the unpolarized component of the light

top_down_rules.title: Verify the diffraction angle equation for single slit
top_down_rules.description: For single-slit diffraction, the condition for minima is given by a*sin(θ) = m*λ, where a is the slit width, θ is the diffraction angle, λ is the wavelength, and m is the order of the minima (m = ±1, ±2, ±3, ...). This equation is valid for angles where sin(θ) does not exceed 1.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the student used the equation a*sin(θ) = m*λ correctly, ensured that |sin(θ)| ≤ 1, and verified that m is a non-zero integer.
common_errors: Using maxima condition instead of minima condition.
Forgetting to check the physical constraint |sin(θ)| ≤ 1.
Incorrectly substituting m or λ values.
Using m = 0, which is not valid for minima.

top_down_rules.title: Verify the double-slit interference condition for maxima
top_down_rules.description: For double-slit interference, the condition for constructive interference (maxima) is d*sin(θ) = m*λ, where d is the distance between the slits, θ is the angle of the maxima, λ is the wavelength, and m is the order of the maxima (m = 0, ±1, ±2, ...).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the equation d*sin(θ) = m*λ is applied for constructive interference, verify the validity of |sin(θ)| ≤ 1, and confirm that m is an integer.
common_errors: Using the minima condition for constructive interference.
Forgetting to check that |sin(θ)| ≤ 1.
Incorrect m values (e.g., non-integer or negative when m = 0 is valid).

top_down_rules.title: Validate the diffraction grating equation
top_down_rules.description: For a diffraction grating, the condition for maxima is given by m*λ = d*sin(θ), where d is the distance between adjacent slits in the grating, θ is the diffraction angle, λ is the wavelength, and m is the diffraction order. This equation is applicable for |sin(θ)| ≤ 1.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the equation m*λ = d*sin(θ) has been used correctly, check the physical constraint |sin(θ)| ≤ 1, and confirm that m is a non-negative integer.
common_errors: Incorrectly calculating d as the number of lines per unit length instead of its reciprocal.
Using the wrong diffraction order m.
Violating the condition |sin(θ)| ≤ 1.

top_down_rules.title: Check the intensity distribution for single-slit diffraction
top_down_rules.description: The intensity in single-slit diffraction is given by I(θ) = I₀ * (sin(β)/β)^2, where β = π*a*sin(θ)/λ, and I₀ is the maximum intensity. This equation describes the variation of intensity with angle and must be used when calculating intensity distributions.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the student uses the correct formula for intensity, substitutes β correctly, and verifies that β is dimensionless. Also, confirm that the intensity is non-negative.
common_errors: Forgetting to square the (sin(β)/β) term.
Incorrectly calculating β.
Using the formula for constructive or destructive interference instead of intensity distribution.
Failing to ensure that intensity values are non-negative.

top_down_rules.title: Verify sign conventions for angles in diffraction problems
top_down_rules.description: In diffraction problems, angles (θ) are measured from the central maximum (θ = 0). Positive angles are typically measured in the counterclockwise direction, and negative angles are measured clockwise. Ensure the correct sign convention is applied when solving for θ.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the student has correctly assigned the sign to θ based on the chosen coordinate system and verified that θ does not exceed ±90° for physical setups.
common_errors: Assigning incorrect signs to angles based on the direction of measurement.
Using θ > 90° or θ < -90°, which violates the physical setup of diffraction.
Confusing the reference point for measuring angles.

top_down_rules.title: Ensure wavelength values are physically valid
top_down_rules.description: In diffraction problems, the wavelength (λ) should correspond to the range of visible or given electromagnetic radiation (e.g., for visible light, 400 nm ≤ λ ≤ 700 nm). Ensure the wavelength is within the given or physically reasonable range.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the value of λ is within the specified range for the problem or the general range for the type of wave considered. Confirm that unit conversions (e.g., nm to meters) are performed correctly.
common_errors: Substituting an invalid or unrealistic wavelength (e.g., negative or out of range).
Using the wrong unit conversion for wavelength (e.g., nm to meters).
Not converting all units to be consistent in the calculation.

top_down_rules.title: Validate the maximum diffraction order for given setup
top_down_rules.description: The diffraction order (m) must satisfy the condition m*λ ≤ d for the given slit spacing (d) and wavelength (λ). This ensures that the angle θ is physically valid (|sin(θ)| ≤ 1).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the maximum diffraction order m_max satisfies m*λ ≤ d, and flag if m exceeds this limit. Ensure that m is a non-negative integer.
common_errors: Using an m value that violates the condition m*λ ≤ d.
Ignoring the maximum diffraction order constraint.
Substituting incorrect values for d or λ.

top_down_rules.title: Check for dimensional and unit consistency in diffraction equations
top_down_rules.description: All terms in the diffraction equations (e.g., a*sin(θ) = m*λ or d*sin(θ) = m*λ) must have consistent units. Wavelength (λ) and slit spacing (a, d) must both be in meters, and angles (θ) should be in radians when used in trigonometric calculations.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that all lengths are converted to meters and that angles are in radians when used with trigonometric functions. Ensure that all terms in the equations have consistent dimensions.
common_errors: Using inconsistent units for wavelength and slit spacing.
Using degrees instead of radians in trigonometric calculations.
Mixing unit systems (e.g., nm for wavelength and cm for slit spacing).

top_down_rules.title: Verify symmetry in diffraction patterns
top_down_rules.description: Diffraction patterns are symmetric about the central maximum. Ensure that the calculated angles and intensities for positive and negative orders (±m) are consistent.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the student has ensured symmetry in the diffraction pattern by verifying that the angles and intensities for ±m are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction.
common_errors: Calculating different angles or intensities for ±m.
Ignoring the symmetry of the diffraction pattern.

top_down_rules.title: Verify Snell's Law for Dispersion
top_down_rules.description: Snell's Law governs the bending of light as it transitions between media with different refractive indices. For dispersion, the refractive index is wavelength-dependent, so ensure n(λ1)sinθ1 = n(λ2)sinθ2 is satisfied for each wavelength.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the sine of the angles and wavelength-dependent refractive indices satisfy Snell's Law for all wavelengths involved. Ensure angles are measured from the normal and refractive indices are correctly assigned for each wavelength.
common_errors: Using constant refractive indices for all wavelengths
Incorrect angle measurement (not measured from the normal)
Omitting the dependence of n on λ

top_down_rules.title: Ensure Correct Functional Form of Refractive Index vs Wavelength
top_down_rules.description: The refractive index of a medium decreases with increasing wavelength in visible light (normal dispersion). Verify that the refractive index assigned to a wavelength follows the expected trend (e.g., Cauchy's equation or Sellmeier equations).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that n(λ) decreases as λ increases within the visible range (400-700 nm). Ensure the chosen equation (e.g., Cauchy or Sellmeier) is appropriate for the material and wavelength range.
common_errors: Assigning increasing refractive index with wavelength
Using an incorrect or oversimplified formula for n(λ)
Misinterpreting the Sellmeier or Cauchy equation parameters

top_down_rules.title: Check Chromatic Aberration Focusing Error
top_down_rules.description: Chromatic aberration occurs because different wavelengths are focused at different points due to the variation in refractive index. Verify that shorter wavelengths (blue light) focus closer to the lens compared to longer wavelengths (red light).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the focal length decreases as wavelength decreases for the lens system under consideration. Ensure the material's dispersion properties are correctly applied.
common_errors: Assuming a single focal point for all wavelengths
Reversing the order of focal points for blue and red light
Ignoring the material's dispersion properties

top_down_rules.title: Verify Angular Dispersion in Prisms
top_down_rules.description: Angular dispersion in a prism arises due to the wavelength dependence of the refractive index. Verify that the angle of deviation increases for shorter wavelengths (e.g., blue light) compared to longer wavelengths (e.g., red light).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that θ_deviation(blue) > θ_deviation(red) for a given prism material and geometry. Verify that the refractive index's wavelength dependence is correctly applied in the deviation angle calculation.
common_errors: Calculating deviation angles without considering wavelength dependence of refractive index
Using incorrect prism angles or geometry
Ignoring the order of angular dispersion for different colors

top_down_rules.title: Verify Dimensional Consistency in Dispersion Equations
top_down_rules.description: Equations governing dispersion (e.g., n = A + B/λ²) must have consistent dimensions. Ensure that terms involving wavelength, refractive index, and material constants are dimensionally compatible.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if all terms in the dispersion equation have consistent physical dimensions and units. Ensure wavelength is converted to meters if necessary.
common_errors: Using incorrect units for wavelength (e.g., nm instead of m)
Omitting the squared term in 1/λ²
Using inconsistent units for dispersion constants

top_down_rules.title: Verify Sign Conventions for Chromatic Aberration
top_down_rules.description: Chromatic aberration calculations often involve focal lengths and distances that use specific sign conventions (e.g., positive for real focal points, negative for virtual). Ensure adherence to these conventions.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the focal lengths and distances are assigned signs correctly based on the lens type (converging/diverging) and image formation. Verify that the sign conventions are consistent throughout the calculation.
common_errors: Using incorrect sign for virtual focal points
Misinterpreting the sign convention for focal lengths
Mixing up sign conventions for converging and diverging lenses

top_down_rules.title: Ensure Applicability of Dispersion Relations to Material
top_down_rules.description: Dispersion relations are material-dependent. Ensure that the equation or model (e.g., Cauchy's equation or Sellmeier equation) is valid for the given material and wavelength range.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the material's dispersion constants or coefficients are appropriate for the wavelength range under consideration. Ensure the material is transparent in the wavelength range being analyzed.
common_errors: Using a dispersion formula outside its valid wavelength range
Applying a dispersion relation to an incorrect material
Ignoring the material's transparency range

top_down_rules.title: Verify Monotonic Decrease of Refractive Index for Normal Dispersion
top_down_rules.description: In normal dispersion, the refractive index decreases monotonically with increasing wavelength. Verify that n(λ) is a decreasing function within the visible spectrum.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if dn/dλ < 0 for all λ in the visible range (400-700 nm). Ensure the data or model used does not imply anomalous dispersion unless explicitly stated.
common_errors: Misinterpreting the trend of refractive index with wavelength
Calculating dn/dλ incorrectly
Using data or models that imply anomalous dispersion without clarification

top_down_rules.title: Verify Anomalous Dispersion Behavior
top_down_rules.description: In regions of anomalous dispersion (e.g., near absorption lines), the refractive index increases with increasing wavelength. Verify that the model or data correctly reflects this behavior if applicable.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if dn/dλ > 0 in regions of anomalous dispersion. Ensure the material and wavelength range are appropriate for this behavior.
common_errors: Assuming normal dispersion in regions of anomalous dispersion
Using incorrect data or models for the material
Ignoring the proximity to absorption lines

top_down_rules.title: Apply Snell's Law for Fiber Entry Angle
top_down_rules.description: Snell's Law governs how light enters an optical fiber, involving the refractive indices of the core and cladding. It determines the critical angle for total internal reflection at the core-cladding interface.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that n_core * sin(theta_core) = n_cladding * sin(theta_cladding). Ensure the entry angle satisfies the conditions for total internal reflection by checking if the angle of incidence is greater than or equal to the critical angle.
common_errors: Incorrect calculation of critical angle
Mixing up refractive indices of core and cladding
Using incorrect sign for angles outside the defined range

top_down_rules.title: Correct Sign Convention for Fiber Alignment
top_down_rules.description: In fiber optics, the direction of light propagation is important. The coordinate system should align positively in the propagation direction and negatively upon reflection, following standard optical conventions.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure the sign convention follows the agreed axis orientation, with positive along the direction of light propagation and negative for reflected directions. Verify that the coordinate system is consistently applied across calculations.
common_errors: Using the wrong axis for propagation direction
Incorrectly reflecting angles, leading to divergence issues
Misalignment of coordinate system leading to miscalculation

top_down_rules.title: Verify Fiber Core Dimension Constraints
top_down_rules.description: Geometric constraints in fiber optics include core diameter and cladding dimensions, which are crucial for guiding light through total internal reflection.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the core diameter is correctly dimensioned relative to the cladding to guide light effectively through total internal reflection. Ensure the numerical aperture (NA) is consistent with the core-cladding ratio.
common_errors: Incorrect ratio of core to cladding sizes
Ignoring the minimal length scales for efficient waveguiding
Miscalculating fiber optic polygon cross-sectional constraints

top_down_rules.title: Ensure Conditions for Total Internal Reflection
top_down_rules.description: Total internal reflection requires the refractive index of the core to be higher than that of the cladding, and angles of incidence greater than the critical angle.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Confirm that the refractive indices satisfy n_core > n_cladding and that the angle of incidence is greater than or equal to the critical angle. Verify that no light escapes through the cladding.
common_errors: Misidentifying pathways for light escape from fiber
Applying TIR concepts without checking refractive index inversion
Overlooking necessary angle conditions leading to leakage

top_down_rules.title: Consistent Dimensions for Fiber Optic Equations
top_down_rules.description: Ensure that dimensions and units are consistent within fiber optic equations, emphasizing the relationship between the speed of light (c), wavelength, and frequency.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that units such as nm (nanometers) for wavelength and GHz for frequency are used correctly in calculations. Ensure dimensional consistency in equations like c = lambda * f and in power loss or dispersion calculations.
common_errors: Unit mismatches: nm for length, GHz for frequency
Misapplying dimensions when calculating power losses or dispersion
Ignoring dimensional consistency in intensity and power calculations

top_down_rules.title: Specify Fiber Material Properties for Application
top_down_rules.description: Different applications require fibers with specific material properties such as attenuation, dispersion, or birefringence. These must be correctly specified for accurate function.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the fiber materials meet specific property requirements for the intended application. Ensure attenuation coefficients, dispersion parameters, and birefringence values are appropriate for the design.
common_errors: Failure to specify suitable materials for intended applications
Neglecting material absorption coefficients
Mistaking material properties leading to operational ineffectiveness

top_down_rules.title: Monitor Speed Limits and Dispersion in Fibers
top_down_rules.description: The speed of light propagation through different media must be monitored to address issues with dispersion and scattering.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that light propagation speeds are within operational constraints. Account for dispersion impacts, including chromatic and modal dispersion, and check for pulse broadening effects over fiber lengths.
common_errors: Overlooking speed consistency checks leading to signal distortion
Neglecting dispersion impact in design calculations
Misrepresenting the pulse propagation characteristics

top_down_rules.title: Assess Bending Loss in Fiber Paths
top_down_rules.description: Bending loss occurs when fibers deviate from straight paths, introducing losses due to reduced conditions for total internal reflection.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Evaluate designs for minimal bends. Ensure that bend radii and angles do not exceed critical thresholds to avoid loss due to mode conversion or leakage.
common_errors: Excessive bending leading to degraded signal
Ignoring bend-induced mode conversion impacts
Miscalculating allowable bend radius

top_down_rules.title: Verify Mode Field Diameter for Single-Mode Fibers
top_down_rules.description: The mode field diameter (MFD) is critical for single-mode fibers, as it determines the spatial distribution of light intensity and affects coupling efficiency.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the MFD is consistent with the fiber's design specifications. Verify that coupling losses are minimized by matching the MFD with the source and detector.
common_errors: Incorrect calculation of mode field diameter
Mismatch between MFD and source/detector dimensions
Overlooking MFD impact on coupling efficiency

top_down_rules.title: Verify Fresnel Diffraction Equation Application
top_down_rules.description: Fresnel diffraction occurs when light diffracts around an object and the wavefront is neither planar nor can be approximated as emanating from a far point source. Ensure that the Fresnel approach is used when the size of the aperture or obstacle is comparable to the wavelength and the distance from the screen to the obstacle is relatively short.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the condition a^2 / (λ * d) > 1 is satisfied, where 'a' is the aperture size, 'λ' is the wavelength, and 'd' is the distance from the aperture to the observation point. Ensure that the aperture size and distance are in the same units.
common_errors: Mistaking Fresnel diffraction conditions with Fraunhofer diffraction
Incorrect assumptions about aperture and distance scales
Using inconsistent units for aperture size, wavelength, and distance

top_down_rules.title: Validate Diffraction Coordinate System
top_down_rules.description: Diffraction problems often use a specific coordinate system, typically with the aperture or obstacle centered at the origin. Ensure correct orientation relative to the incoming wavefront and observation point.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Confirm that the chosen coordinate system aligns with the geometry of the problem, typically with the z-axis along the direction of light propagation. Verify that the aperture or obstacle is centered at the origin and that the observation point is correctly positioned relative to the aperture.
common_errors: Misaligning the coordinate system with the wave direction
Miscalculating angles due to incorrect coordinate setup
Failing to center the aperture or obstacle at the origin

top_down_rules.title: Verify Angular Sign Convention
top_down_rules.description: Diffraction angles must be consistent with the sign convention used, generally proceeding from normal incidence. Positive and negative angles should correlate correctly with the direction of deviation from the incident beam.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure angles are measured from normal incidence, with deviation directions clearly defined (typically positive for deviations to the left and negative for deviations to the right in standard diagrams). Verify that the sign convention is consistent throughout the calculations.
common_errors: Confusing positive and negative diffraction angles
Incorrect angle measurement direction creating calculation errors
Inconsistent use of sign conventions in different parts of the problem

top_down_rules.title: Check Units and Dimensional Consistency
top_down_rules.description: Fresnel and Fraunhofer diffraction calculations involve distances, angles, and wavelengths. Ensure all terms in equations are dimensionally consistent and properly converted between units like meters and nanometers.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Confirm that all calculations using distances, wavelengths, and angles are consistent in units. For example, ensure that the wavelength is converted to meters if distances are given in meters. Verify that all terms in equations have compatible dimensions.
common_errors: Using incorrect wavelength units leading to dimensional inconsistencies
Combining meters and nanometers incorrectly without conversion
Failing to check dimensional consistency in intermediate steps

top_down_rules.title: Ensure Applicable Boundary and Edge Conditions
top_down_rules.description: In diffraction, boundary conditions determine how wavefronts interact with obstacles. Ensure boundary conditions at the edge of apertures or obstacles match the physical setup described.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify the boundary conditions applied correctly reflect the physical edges of the aperture or obstacle, such as zero field intensity at opaque boundaries. Confirm that the boundary conditions are consistent with the mathematical model used.
common_errors: Ignoring boundary effects in diffraction patterns
Inappropriately simplified edge conditions leading to inaccurate diffraction models
