top_down_rules.check_logic: Assess the physical situation to ensure it meets the requirements for treating as a blackbody. Verify that the emissivity is close to 1 for near-perfect blackbodies.
common_errors: Applying blackbody equations to non-blackbody actors
Ignoring the requirement for a blackbody to be a perfect emitter

top_down_rules.title: Verify Geometric Area in Stefan-Boltzmann Calculation
top_down_rules.description: Ensure that the surface area used in calculations accurately represents the radiating object's geometry.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Confirm the surface area (A) is correctly calculated from given geometric parameters before substituting into the equation. For example, use A = 4πr^2 for a sphere.
common_errors: Incorrect calculation or assumption of surface area
Misapplying the geometry of the object in area calculations

top_down_rules.title: Validate Emissivity Value and Range
top_down_rules.description: Check that emissivity (e) is within the physical range of 0 ≤ e ≤ 1, representing a real material's emissive properties.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Confirm emissivity value is within allowable limits before using in Stefan-Boltzmann Law. Ensure emissivity is not confused with reflectivity or absorptivity.
common_errors: Using emissivity values outside the physical range
Confusing emissivity with reflectivity or other optical properties

top_down_rules.title: Correct Sign Convention for Heat Transfer
top_down_rules.description: Check that the sign convention adheres to the principle that energy emitted by radiation from the surface is considered as positive heat loss.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify energy flow direction and ensure heat loss is denoted correctly as a negative contribution in energy balance calculations. Confirm that heat gain is treated as positive.
common_errors: Incorrectly stating energy loss as a gain
Misunderstanding the sign convention in heat balance

top_down_rules.title: Verify Energy Density of Blackbody Radiation
top_down_rules.description: Ensure the energy density of blackbody radiation is calculated correctly using u = (4σ/c)T^4, where c is the speed of light.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the energy density u is calculated using u = (4σ/c)T^4, with T in Kelvin and c as the speed of light in vacuum.
common_errors: Incorrect formula for energy density
Using incorrect value for the speed of light
Temperature not in Kelvin

top_down_rules.title: Verify Radiative Flux Calculation
top_down_rules.description: Ensure the radiative flux (F) is calculated correctly using F = σT^4 for a perfect blackbody.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the radiative flux is calculated using F = σT^4, with T in Kelvin. For non-perfect blackbodies, ensure emissivity is included as F = eσT^4.
common_errors: Neglecting emissivity for non-perfect blackbodies
Using incorrect formula for radiative flux
Temperature not in Kelvin

top_down_rules.title: Apply Carnot Efficiency Formula
top_down_rules.description: The Carnot efficiency equation is used to calculate the maximum efficiency of a heat engine operating between two thermal reservoirs. It is given by η = 1 - (T_cold / T_hot), where T_cold and T_hot are the absolute temperatures of the cold and hot reservoirs, respectively.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Calculate η using η = 1 - (T_cold / T_hot). Ensure that temperatures are in Kelvin and T_hot > T_cold.
common_errors: Using Celsius instead of Kelvin for temperatures
Mixing up T_hot and T_cold
Incorrect subtraction or division order
Using negative temperatures without proper conversion

top_down_rules.title: Verify Reversible Process in Carnot Cycle
top_down_rules.description: A Carnot cycle consists of four reversible processes: two isothermal and two adiabatic. The cycle is hypothetically reversible, and real engines operating on Carnot principles should approach reversibility.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure the process sequence is isothermal expansion, adiabatic expansion, isothermal compression, adiabatic compression. Confirm that no heat exchange occurs during adiabatic processes and that heat exchange occurs only during isothermal processes.
common_errors: Failing to identify the correct sequence of processes
Mistaking any process as irreversible
Incorrectly labeling adiabatic processes as isothermal
Ignoring the reversibility assumption in calculations

top_down_rules.title: Check Temperature Units in Carnot Calculations
top_down_rules.description: Temperatures in thermodynamic calculations involving Carnot cycles must be expressed in absolute units (Kelvin). This ensures correct comparison and ratios in formulas.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify all temperatures are given in Kelvin before substitution into formulas. If temperatures are provided in Celsius, convert them to Kelvin using T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15.
common_errors: Using Celsius or Fahrenheit for temperature inputs
Ignoring unit conversion entirely
Wrong conversion from Celsius to Kelvin
Failing to check for negative temperatures in Celsius

top_down_rules.title: Validate Carnot Cycle Assumptions with Ideal Gas
top_down_rules.description: Carnot engines often assume gases behave ideally in the cycle. This requires conditions where the gas's behavior approximates the ideal gas law closely.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure the problem context or conditions denote ideal gas behavior or provide necessary conditions such as low pressure and high temperature. Verify that the ideal gas law (PV = nRT) is applicable.
common_errors: Assuming ideal behavior when conditions don't support it
Using real gas equations without context clarity
Failing to match conditions with equation assumptions
Ignoring deviations from ideal gas behavior at high pressures or low temperatures

top_down_rules.title: Efficiency Limitation Recognition
top_down_rules.description: The Carnot efficiency represents the maximum efficiency limit for any heat engine operating between two temperatures. No real engine can surpass this efficiency.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Compare calculated engine efficiency with Carnot efficiency (η_c). Report if any real engine efficiency exceeds η_c. Ensure that η_c is calculated correctly using absolute temperatures.
common_errors: Claiming real engine efficiency exceeds Carnot limit
Neglecting the efficiency definition for non-Carnot engines
Misinterpreting efficiency calculations
Failing to account for irreversibilities in real engines

top_down_rules.title: Ensure Work Done Calculations in Adiabatic Processes
top_down_rules.description: In adiabatic processes of a Carnot cycle, work done relies on pressure and volume changes, with no heat exchange occurring.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Evaluate work done using adiabatic relations: W = μ(C_vm/T)*(V_initial/V_final)^(γ-1) where applicable. Confirm that Q = 0 for adiabatic processes.
common_errors: Confusing adiabatic with isochoric processes
Using heat transfer equations in adiabatic calculations
Incorrect exponent calculation involving adiabatic processes
Failing to verify that no heat is exchanged (Q = 0)

top_down_rules.title: Verify Net Power Output Calculation
top_down_rules.description: The net power output of a Carnot engine is calculated from the net work done in one complete cycle, considering all processes.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Calculate net work as W_net = Q_h - Q_c, where Q_h is heat input and Q_c is heat output. Ensure that Q_h > Q_c and that heat values are consistent with the first law of thermodynamics.
common_errors: Incorrectly adding rather than subtracting heats
Omitting work done calculations
Confusion between input and output heat quantities
Failing to check consistency with the first law of thermodynamics

top_down_rules.title: Constrain Cycle Path in P-V Diagram
top_down_rules.description: The Carnot cycle should accurately reflect its adiabatic and isothermal paths in a P-V diagram, depicting ideal process transitions.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure diagram paths are correct: isothermal paths are horizontal while adiabatic paths should curve according to pressure-temperature changes. Verify that transitions between processes are smooth and consistent with thermodynamic principles.
common_errors: Incorrectly labeling isothermal paths as vertical
Misrepresenting adiabatic curves with straight lines
Failing to respect process transitions accurately on diagrams
Ignoring the relationship between pressure, volume, and temperature in the diagram

top_down_rules.title: Verify Heat Transfer in Isothermal Processes
top_down_rules.description: During isothermal processes in the Carnot cycle, heat transfer occurs at constant temperature. The heat absorbed or released is related to the work done.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that Q = W for isothermal processes, where Q is the heat transferred and W is the work done. Verify that the temperature remains constant throughout the process.
common_errors: Failing to equate heat transfer to work done in isothermal processes
Assuming temperature changes during isothermal processes
Ignoring the relationship between heat transfer and work

top_down_rules.title: Verify the differential form of the Clausius-Clapeyron equation
top_down_rules.description: The Clausius-Clapeyron equation in its differential form is written as dP/dT = L / (T * ΔV), where dP/dT is the slope of the phase boundary in a P-T diagram, L is the latent heat of the phase transition, T is the absolute temperature, and ΔV is the change in specific volume between the two phases. This relationship applies at equilibrium between two phases.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure the equation is correctly structured as dP/dT = L / (T * ΔV) with all terms properly substituted.
common_errors: Incorrectly swapping ΔV and L in the equation.
Forgetting to use absolute temperature (T) in Kelvin.
Omitting ΔV or using incorrect phase volumes for ΔV.

top_down_rules.title: Confirm applicability to first-order phase transitions
top_down_rules.description: The Clausius-Clapeyron equation is valid only for first-order phase transitions (e.g., melting, boiling) characterized by a discontinuous change in entropy and volume. It does not apply to second-order transitions or continuous phase changes.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the phase transition is first-order, specifically involving latent heat.
common_errors: Applying the Clausius-Clapeyron equation to second-order phase transitions.
Failure to confirm that the phase transition involves latent heat.

top_down_rules.title: Check dimensional consistency of terms
top_down_rules.description: Ensure all terms in the Clausius-Clapeyron equation have consistent units: L in J/kg or J/mol, T in Kelvin, ΔV in m³/kg or m³/mol, and dP/dT in Pa/K. Dimensional consistency ensures the equation's validity.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify consistency of units for L, T, ΔV, and dP/dT throughout the equation.
common_errors: Using Celsius instead of Kelvin for temperature.
Mismatched units between ΔV and L (e.g., mixing specific and molar quantities).
Omitting unit conversion where necessary (e.g., from bar to Pascal).

top_down_rules.title: Verify correct sign conventions for ΔV and ΔS
top_down_rules.description: Ensure ΔV (change in specific volume) sign matches the phase transition direction. For example, during vaporization, ΔV > 0 (as gas has a larger volume than liquid). Additionally, confirm entropy change ΔS = L/T aligns with heat flow direction.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check that ΔV and ΔS possess the correct signs based on the transition analyzed.
common_errors: Incorrectly assigning ΔV < 0 for vaporization.
Using the wrong sign for ΔS during absorption or release.
Neglecting the physical interpretation of volume changes.

top_down_rules.title: Ensure latent heat is temperature-dependent if specified
top_down_rules.description: In some scenarios, latent heat (L) can vary with temperature. If specified, ensure the correct form L(T) is used in the Clausius-Clapeyron equation.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Confirm whether L is constant or temperature-dependent, using the appropriate form.
common_errors: Assuming constant latent heat when temperature dependence is specified.
Failing to substitute the correct expression for L(T).

top_down_rules.title: Confirm the geometric interpretation on a P-T diagram
top_down_rules.description: The Clausius-Clapeyron equation describes the slope (dP/dT) of the phase boundary on a pressure-temperature (P-T) diagram. Ensure the correct identification of the phase boundary and accurate slope calculation.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify slope (dP/dT) accuracy for the appropriate phase boundary.
common_errors: Analyzing incorrect phase boundary (e.g., melting instead of boiling).
Misinterpreting slope direction on the P-T diagram.

top_down_rules.title: Verify entropy change relation ΔS = L/T
top_down_rules.description: Confirm that the entropy change (ΔS) during a phase transition relates to latent heat (L) as ΔS = L/T, ensuring consistent units and temperature in Kelvin.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Validate correct implementation of ΔS = L/T with consistent units.
common_errors: Neglecting Kelvin temperature conversion before calculating ΔS.
Incorrectly presuming ΔS = L without dividing by T.
Mixing units for L and T (e.g., using Celsius for T).

top_down_rules.title: Verify Energy Expression for Degrees of Freedom
top_down_rules.description: Equipartition theorem states that each degree of freedom contributes (1/2)kT to the internal energy of a system at thermal equilibrium.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the energy associated with each degree of freedom is expressed as (1/2)kT, where k is the Boltzmann constant and T is the absolute temperature. Verify that the factor (1/2) is not omitted and that the degrees of freedom are correctly identified.
common_errors: Using incorrect factor, e.g., forgetting (1/2) factor
Misinterpreting degrees of freedom count

top_down_rules.title: Check Temperature Influence on Energy
top_down_rules.description: The equipartition theorem relates the energy of a system directly to its temperature; energy per degree of freedom linearly increases with temperature.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the energy calculated by the equipartition theorem is directly proportional to the absolute temperature (in Kelvin). Ensure that no non-linear dependencies are introduced.
common_errors: Ignoring the linear dependency on temperature
Using non-absolute temperature scales

top_down_rules.title: Validate Equipartition Application Conditions
top_down_rules.description: Equipartition theorem applies to classical systems where energy is quadratic with coordinate and momentum, and assumes ideal conditions without quantum restrictions.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure the system is classical, the temperature is sufficiently high to avoid quantum effects, and the degrees of freedom involve quadratic energy dependencies. Verify that quantum systems or systems with non-quadratic energy terms are excluded.
common_errors: Applying equipartition theorem to quantum systems improperly
Applying to systems with non-quadratic energy dependencies

top_down_rules.title: Verify Positive Energy Contributions
top_down_rules.description: Energy contributions from degrees of freedom should be positive as temperature and Boltzmann constant are inherently positive.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that all energy contributions calculated from kT are positive. Verify that no negative values arise due to miscalculation of temperature or incorrect sign assignment.
common_errors: Negative energy due to miscalculation of temperature or incorrect sign assignment

top_down_rules.title: Check Dimensional Consistency of Energy and Temperature Variables
top_down_rules.description: The energy given by the equipartition theorem must have correct units, with kT yielding units of energy.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the units of kT align with the units of energy (e.g., Joules in SI units). Ensure that the Boltzmann constant and temperature are expressed in compatible units.
common_errors: Confusing units of temperature (Kelvin vs other scales)
Incorrect unit assignment for Boltzmann constant leading to dimensional inconsistencies

top_down_rules.title: Validate Degree of Freedom Count in the System
top_down_rules.description: The total energy contribution depends on correctly identifying the number of degrees of freedom relevant to the system being considered.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the degree of freedom count matches the physical setup of the system (e.g., 3 for translational per particle, additional for rotations and vibrations). Verify that all relevant degrees of freedom are included and none are omitted.
common_errors: Neglecting rotational or vibrational degrees of freedom
Incorrectly summing degrees of freedom across molecules

top_down_rules.title: Check Kinematic Constraints Affecting Degrees of Freedom
top_down_rules.description: Ensure the system's geometry or constraints do not limit the degrees of freedom expected from theoretical calculations.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that kinematic constraints, such as fixed or constrained components, are accounted for. Adjust the effective degrees of freedom accordingly.
common_errors: Overcounting degrees of freedom by ignoring fixed or constrained components
Missing constraints that reduce effective degrees of freedom

top_down_rules.title: Evaluate Equipartition Theorem in Limiting Cases
top_down_rules.description: Assess application of equipartition theorem in edge cases such as very low temperatures where quantum effects become significant.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check applicability of the theorem in limiting cases where classical assumptions degrade, especially as temperature approaches zero. Ensure that quantum mechanical considerations are applied when necessary.
common_errors: Using classical equipartition in regimes dominated by quantum mechanics
Ignoring quantum restrictions at low temperatures

top_down_rules.title: Verify High-Temperature Limit Behavior
top_down_rules.description: At very high temperatures, the equipartition theorem should remain valid, and quantum effects should become negligible.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the energy contributions per degree of freedom remain consistent with (1/2)kT at high temperatures. Verify that no deviations occur due to incorrect assumptions.
common_errors: Introducing quantum effects unnecessarily at high temperatures
Incorrectly modifying energy contributions at high temperatures

top_down_rules.title: Ensure First Law Equation Utilized
top_down_rules.description: The First Law of Thermodynamics states that the change in internal energy (ΔU) of a system is equal to the heat added to the system (Q) minus the work done by the system (W), expressed as ΔU = Q - W.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify if ΔU = Q - W is used and all variables are defined with correct signs. Ensure the equation is applied consistently across the problem.
common_errors: Using incorrect formula variants like ΔU = W - Q
Confusing heat added with heat removed

top_down_rules.title: Check Direction of Work and Heat
top_down_rules.description: In the First Law of Thermodynamics, heat (Q) added to the system is positive, and work (W) done by the system is positive.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure Q and W have correct signs based on their direction with respect to the system. Verify that heat removed from the system is negative and work done on the system is negative.
common_errors: Inverting signs for heat and work
Confusing work done by the system with work done on the system

top_down_rules.title: Verify Dimensional Consistency
top_down_rules.description: The units for heat (Q), work (W), and change in internal energy (ΔU) must be consistent, typically in Joules (J) in SI units.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure all terms in ΔU = Q - W are expressed in compatible units (e.g., Joules). If other units like calories are used, verify proper conversion.
common_errors: Using different units for heat and work
Mixing energy units like Joules and calories without conversion

top_down_rules.title: Apply Law to Correct System Type
top_down_rules.description: The First Law of Thermodynamics is applicable to closed systems without mass exchange across the boundaries.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the system described is closed and fulfills the criteria for applying the First Law. Ensure no mass flow occurs across the system boundary.
common_errors: Applying First Law to open systems
Ignoring boundary conditions related to mass flow

top_down_rules.title: Constrain Equation for Isothermal Process
top_down_rules.description: In an isothermal process for ideal gases, the change in internal energy (ΔU) is zero, so Q = W.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify if ΔU = 0 is correctly applied and Q = W condition is met for ideal gas isothermal processes. Ensure the gas is ideal and the process is truly isothermal.
common_errors: Misapplying isothermal condition to non-ideal gases
Forgetting ΔU = 0 for isothermal processes

top_down_rules.title: Adiabatic Process Application
top_down_rules.description: For adiabatic processes, no heat is exchanged (Q=0), and the First Law simplifies to ΔU = -W.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure Q=0 is correctly applied in adiabatic calculations and ΔU = -W is used. Verify that the process is truly adiabatic (no heat exchange).
common_errors: Incorrectly setting Q≠0 for adiabatic cases
Misunderstanding work direction for adiabatic processes

top_down_rules.title: Verify Closed Cycle Conditions
top_down_rules.description: In a closed thermodynamic cycle, the net change in internal energy is zero, so Σ(Q - W) = 0.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that calculations for cycles result in ΣΔU = 0, checking each step in the cycle. Verify that the system returns to its initial state.
common_errors: Failing to sum cycle stages correctly
Ignoring net zero change in internal energy for cycles

top_down_rules.title: Differentiate Types of Work
top_down_rules.description: Recognize different types of work (e.g., PV work) and ensure appropriate application in the First Law.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Distinguish between work types (PV work versus other forms) and apply correctly in ΔU = Q - W. Verify that the correct work expression is used for the given process.
common_errors: Confusing PV work with electrical work
Ignoring the specificity of work types in energy calculations

top_down_rules.title: Verify Heat Transfer Mode
top_down_rules.description: Ensure the mode of heat transfer (conduction, convection, or radiation) is consistent with the problem's context.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the heat transfer mode is correctly identified and applied in the calculation of Q. Verify that assumptions about heat transfer are valid.
common_errors: Assuming conduction when radiation dominates
Ignoring mixed modes of heat transfer

top_down_rules.title: Account for Non-Ideal Gas Behavior
top_down_rules.description: For non-ideal gases, ensure that deviations from ideal gas behavior are considered in thermodynamic calculations.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify if corrections for non-ideal gas behavior (e.g., van der Waals equation) are applied when necessary. Ensure that ideal gas assumptions are not incorrectly used.
common_errors: Using ideal gas law for non-ideal gases
Ignoring intermolecular forces and finite molecular volume

experience_rules.topic: First Law of Thermodynamics
experience_rules.title: 真空边界与弹簧原长平衡态判定
experience_rules.trigger: 题目提及“真空(vacuum)”与“弹簧原长(natural length)”
experience_rules.check_logic: 确认初始或特定状态下气体压力P是否由弹簧弹力唯一提供；若另一侧为真空，则P·A = k·Δx 恒成立。

experience_rules.topic: First Law of Thermodynamics
experience_rules.title: 可动边界热力学系统建模
experience_rules.trigger: 题目涉及“frictionless piston”且存在热交换或温度变化时
experience_rules.check_logic: 检查能量守恒方程是否包含功项 P*dV/dt，不能简单套用 dQ = n*Cv*dT，需结合理想气体状态方程和两侧压力平衡约束。

experience_rules.topic: First Law of Thermodynamics
experience_rules.title: 弹簧约束下气体的等效热容建模
experience_rules.trigger: 理想气体压力受线性弹簧约束（P ∝ x）且需计算比热/热容时
experience_rules.check_logic: 利用P=kx/A和PV=RT，对P(V)V=RT求全微分，寻找PdV与RdT的比例关系，代入第一定律dQ=dU+PdV求解。

experience_rules.topic: First Law of Thermodynamics
experience_rules.title: 不可逆绝热过程禁用状态方程幂函数
experience_rules.trigger: 题目描述中出现“irreversible”、“adiabatic”且涉及理想气体的初末态关联时。
experience_rules.check_logic: 禁止直接使用 $PV^\gamma=const$ 或 $TV^{\gamma-1}=const$；必须改用热力学第一定律 $\Delta U = W + Q$（此处 $Q=0$）进行能量守恒建模。

experience_rules.topic: First Law of Thermodynamics
experience_rules.title: 多腔室耦合瞬态变化率
experience_rules.trigger: 涉及两个由活塞隔开的腔室计算初始变化率 (dT/dt, dV/dt) 时
experience_rules.check_logic: 必须建立联立方程组：能量守恒（两室）、压力平衡（P1=P2）及其导数、体积约束（V1+V2=const）。

experience_rules.topic: First Law of Thermodynamics
experience_rules.title: 含重力活塞系统的能量守恒建模
experience_rules.trigger: 绝热容器中含有重力活塞且发生位移时。
experience_rules.check_logic: 检查方程是否包含：气体内能增量 $\Delta U$、活塞重力势能变化 $mg\Delta h$、以及恒定外压做功 $p_0 A \Delta h$ 的平衡关系。

top_down_rules.title: Verify heat engine efficiency equation
top_down_rules.description: The efficiency of a heat engine is given by η = 1 - (Qc/Qh), where Qh is the heat absorbed from the hot reservoir and Qc is the heat rejected to the cold reservoir. This relation assumes a cyclic process.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if η = 1 - (Qc/Qh) is correctly applied, ensuring Qh > Qc > 0 and all terms are positive.
common_errors: Incorrect placement of Qc and Qh in the formula.
Assigning negative values to Qc or Qh, violating the assumption of heat as a positive quantity.
Calculating η > 1, which is physically impossible.

top_down_rules.title: Validate Coefficient of Performance (COP) for refrigerators
top_down_rules.description: The COP of a refrigerator is defined as COP = Qc / W, where Qc is the heat extracted from the cold reservoir and W is the work done on the system.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that COP is calculated as COP = Qc/W, where Qc > 0 and W > 0, and verify that the result is physically meaningful (COP > 0).
common_errors: Misinterpreting the formula and using Qh instead of Qc.
Using a negative value for work done (W), which is inconsistent with the definition.
Calculating COP < 0, which is unphysical.

top_down_rules.title: Apply the First Law of Thermodynamics
top_down_rules.description: The first law states ΔU = Q - W, where ΔU is the change in internal energy, Q is the heat added to the system, and W is the work done by the system. This law must hold for any thermodynamic process.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the energy balance ΔU = Q - W is used, all terms have consistent units, and the sign convention is correctly applied.
common_errors: Forgetting to account for all forms of energy transfer (Q or W).
Incorrect sign convention for work (e.g., using W as work done on the system instead of by the system).
Ignoring ΔU when it is non-zero for non-cyclic processes.

top_down_rules.title: Check Carnot efficiency limits
top_down_rules.description: The Carnot efficiency is the theoretical maximum efficiency for a heat engine operating between two temperatures, given by η_Carnot = 1 - (Tc/Th), where Tc and Th are the absolute temperatures of the cold and hot reservoirs, respectively.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that η_Carnot = 1 - (Tc/Th) is used, with Tc < Th and temperatures expressed in Kelvin. Verify that η_Carnot ≤ 1.
common_errors: Using temperatures in Celsius instead of Kelvin.
Switching Tc and Th, leading to unphysical negative efficiency.
Calculating η_Carnot > 1, which violates the second law of thermodynamics.

top_down_rules.title: Ensure consistent sign conventions for heat and work
top_down_rules.description: In thermodynamics, heat (Q) is positive when added to the system, and work (W) is positive when done by the system. Misinterpreting these conventions can lead to incorrect calculations.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that Q is positive for heat input and W is positive for work output. For refrigerators, W is positive for work done on the system. Ensure consistency across all calculations.
common_errors: Using opposite sign conventions for Q and W.
Confusing work done by the system with work done on the system.
Neglecting to check signs in cyclic processes.

top_down_rules.title: Verify compliance with the Kelvin-Planck statement
top_down_rules.description: The Kelvin-Planck statement of the second law of thermodynamics states that it is impossible to construct a heat engine that operates in a cycle and converts all the heat absorbed into work (i.e., W cannot equal Qh).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if W < Qh for any heat engine operating in a cycle. Ensure that some heat is always rejected to the cold reservoir (Qc > 0).
common_errors: Assuming 100% conversion of heat to work (W = Qh).
Ignoring losses to the cold reservoir (Qc).
Violating the second law by assuming η = 1.

top_down_rules.title: Check conditions for reversible processes
top_down_rules.description: A thermodynamic process is reversible if it is quasi-static and there are no dissipative forces (e.g., friction, turbulence). Reversible processes are idealized and maximize efficiency.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that processes assumed to be reversible have no dissipative forces, occur quasi-statically, and involve infinitesimally small temperature gradients for heat transfer.
common_errors: Assuming reversibility for real-world processes with friction or turbulence.
Overlooking the need for infinitesimally small temperature gradients for heat transfer.

top_down_rules.title: Ensure dimensional and unit consistency
top_down_rules.description: In thermodynamic equations, all terms must have consistent units (e.g., Q, W, and ΔU in joules, temperatures in Kelvin). Incorrect units can cause significant errors in calculations.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that all terms in equations have compatible units (joules for energy, Kelvin for temperature, etc.). Ensure proper unit conversions where necessary.
common_errors: Using Celsius instead of Kelvin in temperature ratios.
Mixing different energy units (e.g., joules and calories) without conversion.
Failing to convert work or heat into consistent energy units.

top_down_rules.title: Verify entropy change calculations
top_down_rules.description: The change in entropy (ΔS) for a reversible process is given by ΔS = Qrev/T, where Qrev is the reversible heat transfer and T is the absolute temperature. For irreversible processes, ΔS > Q/T.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that ΔS = Qrev/T is used for reversible processes, and verify that ΔS ≥ 0 for all processes, consistent with the second law of thermodynamics.
common_errors: Using Q instead of Qrev for entropy calculations in reversible processes.
Calculating ΔS < 0 for an isolated system, violating the second law.
Ignoring the temperature dependence of entropy changes.

top_down_rules.title: Apply Fourier's Law for Heat Conduction
top_down_rules.description: Fourier's Law states that the heat transfer rate (q) through a material is proportional to the temperature gradient and is given by q = -k * A * (dT/dx), where k is the thermal conductivity, A is the cross-sectional area, and dT/dx is the temperature gradient. This applies to steady-state, one-dimensional heat conduction.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the heat transfer rate is computed using q = -k * A * (dT/dx), that k, A, and dT/dx are correctly defined, and that the negative sign is used to indicate heat flows from high to low temperature.
common_errors: Incorrect sign: forgetting the negative sign indicating heat flows from high to low temperature.
Using incorrect or inconsistent units for thermal conductivity (k).
Forgetting to account for the cross-sectional area (A).
Misinterpreting the temperature gradient direction.

top_down_rules.title: Apply Newton's Law of Cooling for Convection
top_down_rules.description: Newton's Law of Cooling states that the convective heat transfer rate (q) is proportional to the temperature difference between the surface and the surrounding fluid: q = h * A * (T_surface - T_fluid), where h is the convective heat transfer coefficient, A is the surface area, and T_surface/T_fluid are the temperatures of the surface and fluid, respectively.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure q is calculated using q = h * A * (T_surface - T_fluid), that all variables are correctly defined and evaluated, and that the temperature difference is calculated with the correct sign.
common_errors: Omitting the surface area (A) in the formula.
Using inconsistent units for the convective heat transfer coefficient (h).
Incorrectly calculating the temperature difference (e.g., wrong sign).
Applying the law when fluid motion or convection is not present.

top_down_rules.title: Apply Stefan-Boltzmann Law for Radiation
top_down_rules.description: The Stefan-Boltzmann Law states that the radiative heat transfer rate (q) from a surface is proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature: q = ε * σ * A * (T_surface^4 - T_surroundings^4), where ε is the emissivity, σ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, A is the surface area, and T_surface/T_surroundings are absolute temperatures (in Kelvin).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that q is calculated using q = ε * σ * A * (T_surface^4 - T_surroundings^4), that temperatures are in Kelvin, and that emissivity (ε) is correctly applied.
common_errors: Forgetting to convert temperatures to Kelvin.
Mistaking emissivity (ε) as 1 when it's not explicitly stated.
Incorrectly raising temperatures to the fourth power.
Ignoring the surface area (A) in the calculation.

top_down_rules.title: Use Thermal Resistance Networks for Composite Systems
top_down_rules.description: In steady-state heat conduction across composite systems, the equivalent thermal resistance can be used to simplify the calculation. For series systems, R_eq = R1 + R2 + ...; for parallel systems, 1/R_eq = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + .... Thermal resistance is defined as R = L/(k*A), where L is the material thickness.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure thermal resistance is calculated correctly for series or parallel systems, combined appropriately to find the equivalent resistance, and that all layers or paths in the composite system are considered.
common_errors: Adding thermal resistances incorrectly for parallel configurations.
Using incorrect expressions for thermal resistance (e.g., forgetting the A term).
Mixing up series and parallel configurations.
Not considering all layers or paths in the composite system.

top_down_rules.title: Use Correct Sign Conventions for Heat Flow
top_down_rules.description: Heat flow is typically considered positive when it flows into a system and negative when it flows out. The chosen sign convention must remain consistent throughout the problem.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the sign convention for heat flow is consistently applied across all calculations and matches the physical scenario.
common_errors: Inconsistently assigning heat flow as positive or negative.
Forgetting to account for the chosen sign convention in intermediate steps.
Reversing the sign of heat flow in composite systems.

top_down_rules.title: Check Validity Conditions for Heat Transfer Equations
top_down_rules.description: Heat transfer equations (conduction, convection, radiation) have specific conditions for validity. Fourier's Law requires steady-state conduction, Newton's Law of Cooling assumes convective heat transfer, and Stefan-Boltzmann Law applies to radiative heat transfer in the absence of significant convection or conduction.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure the heat transfer equation used is valid for the given physical conditions (e.g., steady state, type of heat transfer mechanism, absence of dominating alternate mechanisms).
common_errors: Using Fourier's Law when the system is not in steady state.
Applying Newton's Law of Cooling in the absence of fluid convection.
Using the Stefan-Boltzmann Law when conduction or convection dominates the heat transfer.

top_down_rules.title: Ensure Dimensional Consistency in Heat Transfer Equations
top_down_rules.description: Each term in the heat transfer equations must have consistent units. For example, in q = -k * A * (dT/dx), the units of q must match the product of k, A, and dT/dx.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that all terms in the heat transfer equations have consistent units (e.g., energy/time or power) and that unit conversions are correctly applied.
common_errors: Using inconsistent units for thermal conductivity (e.g., W/mK vs. W/cmK).
Neglecting to convert area or length units to match the desired unit system.
Incorrectly converting temperature gradients (e.g., Celsius per meter vs. Kelvin per meter).

top_down_rules.title: Apply Correct Boundary Conditions
top_down_rules.description: Heat transfer problems often involve specific boundary conditions, such as constant temperature, constant heat flux, or convection at the boundary. These must be correctly incorporated into the solution.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the boundary conditions are correctly applied, match the physical scenario, and are consistently used in solving the heat transfer equations.
common_errors: Misinterpreting or omitting boundary conditions.
Incorrectly applying a constant heat flux boundary condition.
Failing to match boundary conditions with the physical scenario (e.g., mixing convection and insulation).

top_down_rules.title: Account for Transient Heat Transfer
top_down_rules.description: In non-steady-state heat transfer, the temperature changes with time and must be modeled using transient heat transfer equations, such as the heat diffusion equation or lumped capacitance method.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that transient heat transfer equations are used when the system is not in steady state and that initial and boundary conditions are correctly applied.
common_errors: Using steady-state equations for transient problems.
Ignoring initial conditions or time-dependent boundary conditions.
Incorrectly applying the lumped capacitance method when Biot number is not small.

topics.topic: Ideal Gas Law and Real Gas Behavior

top_down_rules.title: Verify Ideal Gas Law Formulation
top_down_rules.description: The ideal gas law is expressed as PV = nRT, where P is pressure, V is volume, n is the number of moles, R is the universal gas constant, and T is temperature in kelvins. This relationship applies to ideal gases under standard conditions.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure the equation is explicitly written as PV = nRT with all variables correctly assigned and units suitable for the context.
common_errors: Using incorrect units for R (e.g., J/mol·K with P in atm)
Failure to convert temperature to kelvins
Misplacing or misinterpreting variables within the equation

top_down_rules.title: Ensure Temperature is in Kelvins
top_down_rules.description: The ideal gas law requires the absolute temperature in kelvins. Celsius or Fahrenheit must be converted to kelvins using T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the temperature has been converted to kelvins before using it in the ideal gas equation and note any errors in conversion.
common_errors: Using Celsius or Fahrenheit directly in calculations
Forgetting to add 273.15 when converting from Celsius to kelvins

top_down_rules.title: Check Dimensional Consistency of Ideal Gas Law
top_down_rules.description: Each term in the ideal gas law must have consistent units. For example, P in Pascals, V in cubic meters, n in moles, T in kelvins, and R in J/(mol·K).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that units for each variable are coherent and consistent throughout calculations, especially when mixing English and SI units.
common_errors: Mixing units that are not compatible (e.g., atm for pressure and cubic meters for volume)
Using non-SI units without proper conversion

top_down_rules.title: Check Validity of Ideal Gas Law Assumptions
top_down_rules.description: The ideal gas law assumes negligible intermolecular forces and that gas particles occupy no volume. It is valid at low pressures and high temperatures where these assumptions are close.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Evaluate the pressure and temperature conditions of the problem and determine the appropriateness of applying the ideal gas law.
common_errors: Applying the ideal gas law to high-pressure or low-temperature scenarios
Ignoring intermolecular forces in dense gases

top_down_rules.title: Consider Real Gas Corrections (Van der Waals Equation)
top_down_rules.description: For real gases, the Van der Waals equation (P + a(n/V)^2)(V - nb) = nRT accounts for intermolecular forces and finite particle volume. Use this equation under non-ideal conditions.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Determine if the problem presents conditions that require accounting for real gas behavior, notably at high pressure or low temperature.
common_errors: Using the ideal gas law when real gas behavior is significant
Neglecting correction terms a and b

top_down_rules.title: Verify Work Sign Convention in Gas Expansion/Compression
top_down_rules.description: When a gas expands, work is done by the gas, and W is positive. When compressed, work is done on the gas, and W is negative.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Confirm the direction of work based on volume changes to apply correct sign convention, ensuring consistency with the first law of thermodynamics.
common_errors: Flipping the sign of work
Inconsistencies in work calculations within the context of ΔU = Q - W

top_down_rules.title: Verify Constraints for Isothermal, Isobaric, Isochoric, and Adiabatic Processes
top_down_rules.description: Verify fixed or zero values for properties specific to these processes: T constant for isothermal, P constant for isobaric, V constant for isochoric, and Q = 0 for adiabatic process.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure the correct variable is being treated according to the type of process and verify constraints are appropriately applied.
common_errors: Not maintaining constant temperature in isothermal processes
Neglecting Q = 0 in adiabatic processes
Failing to maintain P or V constant in isobaric or isochoric processes

top_down_rules.title: Check Molar Mass and Mass-Volume Conversions
top_down_rules.description: Verify correct calculation of mole number using n = m/M, where m is mass and M is molar mass, important for correct use in gas law equations.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Confirm the mass and volume conversions, ensuring the molar mass is accurate and correctly used to convert mass to moles.
common_errors: Omitting division of mass by molar mass
Utilizing incorrect molar mass figures

top_down_rules.title: Check Entropy Change Calculations in Thermodynamic Processes
top_down_rules.description: Ensure correct assessment of entropy changes (ΔS) based on process type and whether the gas is ideal or real.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Evaluate entropy changes considering the process specifics, such as temperature changes and phase transitions, applicable to ideal and real gas scenarios.
common_errors: Ignoring factors impacting entropy change
Assuming no entropy change during irreversible processes without proper justification

top_down_rules.title: Verify Ideal Gas Law Application
top_down_rules.description: The Ideal Gas Law PV = nRT relates pressure (P), volume (V), number of moles (n), and temperature (T). It applies to ideal gases, which are assumed to have perfectly elastic collisions and negligible volume occupied by the gas particles.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure the problem conditions specify an ideal gas, often monoatomic and low-pressure conditions. Check if all the variables in PV = nRT are accounted for, and verify units: P in pascal, V in cubic meters, n in moles, R = 8.314 J/mol·K, and T in Kelvin.
common_errors: Using Celsius instead of Kelvin for temperature
Incorrect unit conversion for pressure or volume
Omitting gas constant R
Confusion between atmospheric pressure and pressure in pascal

top_down_rules.title: Calculate Average Kinetic Energy per Molecule
top_down_rules.description: Average kinetic energy per molecule in an ideal gas is given by (3/2)kT, where k is Boltzmann's constant and T is absolute temperature.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that temperature is expressed in Kelvin and k is correctly used as 1.38 x 10^-23 J/K. Check dimensional consistency for energy output in joules.
common_errors: Using Celsius instead of Kelvin
Misplacement of 3/2 factor in kinetic energy calculation
Incorrect value or units for Boltzmann's constant

top_down_rules.title: Verify Maxwell-Boltzmann Distribution Assumptions
top_down_rules.description: Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution describes the distribution of speeds of particles in a gas at a given temperature. It assumes non-interacting and identical particles.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure the system being analyzed is monoatomic and exhibits classical behavior, no quantum effects. This distribution is valid for a large number of particles and at thermal equilibrium.
common_errors: Incorrectly applying Maxwell-Boltzmann to quantum or interacting systems
Calculations outside validity range

top_down_rules.title: Verify Mean Free Path Calculation
top_down_rules.description: Mean free path is the average distance traveled by a molecule between collisions. Use the formula λ = kT / (sqrt(2) * π * d^2 * P), where d is the molecular diameter.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check units: λ in meters, diameter d in meters, pressure P in pascal, temperature T in Kelvin. Ensure conditions describe an ideal gas scenario.
common_errors: Incorrect diameter units
Failing to include sqrt(2) factor
Using non-ideal gas conditions
Incorrect conditions for low density or high temperature cases

top_down_rules.title: Relate Temperature to Internal Energy
top_down_rules.description: For a monoatomic ideal gas, internal energy U is proportional to temperature T as U = (3/2)nRT. This applies only to monoatomic gases.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Confirm the gas type is monoatomic and temperature is clearly defined in Kelvin. Ensure correct usage of mole quantity n and gas constant R.
common_errors: Applying relation to non-monoatomic gases
Misinterpretation of temperature scale
Neglecting mole count or incorrect R
Incorrect conditions for systems at very high or low temperatures

top_down_rules.title: Validate Degrees of Freedom in Energy Distribution
top_down_rules.description: Equipartition theorem states that each degree of freedom contributes (1/2)kT to the energy for ideal gases.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure degrees of freedom are correctly determined based on molecular structure (e.g., 3 translational for monoatomic gases).
common_errors: Incorrect count of degrees of freedom
Misapplication of (1/2)kT per degree of freedom
Wrong assumption for polyatomic gases
Not accounting for rotational and vibrational degrees in complex molecules

top_down_rules.title: Check Dimensional Consistency in Calculations
top_down_rules.description: All calculated dimensions and units for derived quantities from kinetic theory must be consistent (e.g., pressure in pascal, volume in m^3, temperature in Kelvin).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Review each equation and result for dimensional consistency using SI units. Flag conversion errors for immediate correction.
common_errors: Mixing units (e.g., liters vs m^3 for volume)
Temperature in Celsius leading to inconsistent dimensions
Pressure in atm instead of pascal without conversion
Neglecting standard conditions definitions, leading to confusion

top_down_rules.title: Verify Thermal Boundary Conditions
top_down_rules.description: Ensure that thermal boundary conditions are properly defined and adhered to, concerning ideal and real gas behaviors.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Identify whether boundary conditions for pressure, volume, and temperature are specified and align with thermodynamic assumptions for ideal gases.
common_errors: Ignoring effects of container materials affecting thermal boundaries
Assuming perfectly insulated systems without specification
Omitting consideration of external temperature fluctuations

top_down_rules.title: Verify correct partial derivative relationships in Maxwell's relations
top_down_rules.description: Maxwell's relations originate from the symmetry of second derivatives in thermodynamic potentials. Ensure that the correct partial derivatives are used, such as (∂T/∂V)_S = -(∂P/∂S)_V.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if the second mixed partial derivatives of the thermodynamic potentials are correctly equated. For example, verify that (∂²G/∂T∂P) = (∂²G/∂P∂T). Ensure that the variables and signs are consistent with the specific Maxwell relation being used.
common_errors: Incorrect variable pairings (e.g., swapping T and S when differentiating)
Omitting the minus sign in some relations
Using the wrong thermodynamic potential for the given variables

top_down_rules.title: Ensure thermodynamic equilibrium for Maxwell's relations application
top_down_rules.description: Maxwell's relations are derived under the assumption of thermodynamic equilibrium. Check if the system satisfies equilibrium conditions, such as constant temperature, pressure, or no net heat flow.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the problem statement explicitly mentions thermodynamic equilibrium or conditions implying equilibrium (e.g., constant T, P, or volume). Ensure that transient or irreversible processes are not mistakenly analyzed using Maxwell's relations.
common_errors: Applying Maxwell's relations to systems not in equilibrium
Ignoring transient or irreversible processes

top_down_rules.title: Check dimension/unit consistency in Maxwell's relations
top_down_rules.description: Maxwell's relations involve quantities like temperature (T), entropy (S), pressure (P), volume (V), and energy (E). Ensure that the units or dimensions of derivatives match (e.g., (∂T/∂V)_S has units of T/V).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the units of the partial derivatives are consistent with the definition of the thermodynamic state function. For example, (∂P/∂T)_V should have units of pressure/temperature. Ensure that unit conversions, if any, are handled correctly.
common_errors: Mismatch in units of variables during differentiation
Incorrectly handling unit conversion factors (e.g., for entropy in different units)

top_down_rules.title: Verify correct sign conventions in Maxwell's relations
top_down_rules.description: Sign conventions in thermodynamics are crucial. For example, entropy increases (+) when heat is added to the system, and work done by the system decreases energy (-).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that negative signs are placed correctly in Maxwell's relations, such as - (∂P/∂S)_V or - (∂T/∂V)_S. Ensure that the sign conventions align with the physical interpretation of the thermodynamic quantities.
common_errors: Forgetting the negative sign in the relation
Reversing the sign of work or entropy changes

top_down_rules.title: Ensure compatibility of thermodynamic potentials with chosen Maxwell relation
top_down_rules.description: Maxwell's relations are derived from specific thermodynamic potentials (U, H, G, A). Verify that the chosen relation corresponds to the correct potential.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the thermodynamic potential used matches the relation. For example, (∂S/∂V)_T is derived from Helmholtz free energy (A). Ensure that the potential is correctly identified based on the variables involved.
common_errors: Using Gibbs free energy (G) instead of Helmholtz free energy (A)
Applying the wrong potential to the given variable set

top_down_rules.title: Check if boundary conditions are consistent with Maxwell's relations
top_down_rules.description: Maxwell's relations often involve fixed variables (e.g., constant T, P, or V). Ensure the problem statement specifies these conditions for the relation to hold.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the fixed variables (e.g., constant T or V) are explicitly stated or implied in the problem. Ensure that the chosen Maxwell relation corresponds to the specified boundary conditions.
common_errors: Applying the wrong Maxwell relation due to misunderstanding fixed variables
Omitting the constraint condition entirely

top_down_rules.title: Verify geometric constraints for volume-related Maxwell relations
top_down_rules.description: When using Maxwell's relations involving volume (V), ensure that the system has well-defined and physically meaningful geometric constraints (e.g., no negative volume).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check that the volume is positive and finite, and physically plausible constraints (like incompressibility) are respected. Ensure that the geometric constraints are consistent with the thermodynamic assumptions.
common_errors: Allowing negative or zero volume in calculations
Neglecting imposed constraints like incompressibility or boundary limits

top_down_rules.title: Ensure statistical mechanics consistency in derivation of Maxwell's relations
top_down_rules.description: Maxwell's relations can be derived from statistical mechanics. Verify that the macroscopic thermodynamic quantities used (e.g., S, T, P) are consistent with the statistical interpretation (e.g., entropy from microstates).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Confirm the thermodynamic quantities align with their statistical definitions, such as S = k_B ln(Ω). Ensure that the Boltzmann constant (k_B) and other statistical parameters are used consistently.
common_errors: Misinterpreting entropy as heat instead of its statistical definition
Inconsistent use of Boltzmann constant (k_B) in units or calculations

top_down_rules.title: Verify numerical implementation of Maxwell's relations
top_down_rules.description: When Maxwell's relations are used in numerical calculations, ensure that the numerical methods (e.g., finite differences) are implemented correctly.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that numerical approximations of derivatives (e.g., ∂P/∂T) are consistent with the analytical expressions. Check for proper handling of numerical precision and rounding errors.
common_errors: Incorrect numerical differentiation methods
Ignoring numerical precision issues leading to significant errors

top_down_rules.title: Ensure correctness of Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution equation
top_down_rules.description: The Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution is given by f(v) = 4π * (m / 2πkT)^(3/2) * v^2 * exp(-mv^2 / 2kT). This equation describes the probability density of molecular speeds in an ideal gas at thermal equilibrium. It applies only to ideal gases where intermolecular interactions are negligible.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the provided equation matches the standard form, including all terms, exponents, and the exponential factor. Ensure that the equation is dimensionally consistent.
common_errors: Omitting the factor of 4π in the equation
Incorrect exponent in the term (m / 2πkT)
Forgetting the v^2 term in the equation
Misplacing or misinterpreting the exponential factor (-mv^2 / 2kT)

top_down_rules.title: Check unit consistency in Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution
top_down_rules.description: In the Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution, ensure that the units are consistent: m should be in kg, k (Boltzmann constant) in J/K, T in K, and v in m/s. The overall units of f(v) should be 1/(m/s), as it's a probability density over speed.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the units of each term in the equation are consistent and that f(v) has units of 1/(m/s). Ensure that all constants and variables are expressed in SI units.
common_errors: Mixing units of mass (e.g., using grams instead of kilograms)
Using incorrect units for Boltzmann constant (e.g., not converting to J/K)
Forgetting to ensure that temperature is in Kelvin

top_down_rules.title: Ensure correct calculation of mean speed
top_down_rules.description: The mean speed for the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution is given by ⟨v⟩ = sqrt(8kT / πm). This is derived by integrating the speed distribution function. It applies only to ideal gases in thermal equilibrium.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the mean speed is calculated using ⟨v⟩ = sqrt(8kT / πm) and that all terms are correctly substituted. Ensure that the units of the result are consistent with m/s.
common_errors: Incorrect formula for mean speed (e.g., using root-mean-square speed instead)
Forgetting the factor of sqrt(8/π)
Not substituting temperature or mass correctly into the formula

top_down_rules.title: Ensure correct calculation of root-mean-square (RMS) speed
top_down_rules.description: The root-mean-square speed in the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution is given by v_rms = sqrt(3kT / m). This represents the square root of the average of the speed squared and applies only to ideal gases in thermal equilibrium.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the RMS speed is calculated using v_rms = sqrt(3kT / m) and that all terms are correctly substituted. Ensure that the units of the result are consistent with m/s.
common_errors: Confusing RMS speed with mean speed or most probable speed
Forgetting the factor of sqrt(3)
Misplacing variables (e.g., swapping m and kT)

top_down_rules.title: Ensure correct calculation of most probable speed
top_down_rules.description: The most probable speed in the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution is given by v_mp = sqrt(2kT / m). This is the speed at which the probability density f(v) is maximized. It applies only to ideal gases in thermal equilibrium.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the most probable speed is calculated using v_mp = sqrt(2kT / m) and that all terms are correctly substituted. Ensure that the units of the result are consistent with m/s.
common_errors: Using incorrect formula for v_mp (e.g., confusing it with mean or RMS speed)
Forgetting the factor of sqrt(2)
Not verifying the maximization condition for f(v)

top_down_rules.title: Check validity conditions for Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution
top_down_rules.description: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution applies only to ideal gases in thermal equilibrium. It assumes negligible intermolecular interactions, classical mechanics (non-relativistic speeds), and a continuous spectrum of molecular speeds.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the problem specifies an ideal gas at thermal equilibrium and that the given conditions satisfy classical mechanics (v << c). Ensure that the system is not quantum mechanical (e.g., Bose-Einstein or Fermi-Dirac statistics).
common_errors: Applying Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution to non-ideal gases
Assuming the distribution holds at relativistic speeds (v ~ c)
Using the distribution for quantum systems (e.g., Bose-Einstein or Fermi-Dirac statistics)

top_down_rules.title: Perform dimensional analysis for Maxwell-Boltzmann-related calculations
top_down_rules.description: All derived quantities from the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution — such as mean speed, RMS speed, and most probable speed — must have the correct dimensional consistency. The derived speed formulae must have units of m/s.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the derived expressions for speed (mean, RMS, most probable) yield units of m/s, and that all intermediate terms are dimensionally consistent. Verify that constants like k and m are expressed in SI units.
common_errors: Incorrect units in intermediate calculations (e.g., using temperature in Celsius instead of Kelvin)
Not verifying the dimensions of the Boltzmann constant
Forgetting to ensure consistent units for mass and speed

top_down_rules.title: Check normalization of Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution
top_down_rules.description: The Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution must integrate over all speeds to 1 (normalization).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the distribution integrates to 1 over all speeds. Ensure that the integration limits are correct and that the normalization constant is properly included.
common_errors: Forgetting to normalize the distribution
Incorrect integration limits for verifying normalization
Neglecting the normalization constant in the equation

top_down_rules.title: Verify peak of Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution
top_down_rules.description: The Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution should peak at the most probable speed (v_mp).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that the derivative of the distribution function f(v) with respect to v is zero at v = v_mp, confirming that the peak occurs at the most probable speed.
common_errors: Not verifying the derivative condition for the peak
Incorrect calculation of the most probable speed
Assuming the peak occurs at mean or RMS speed instead of v_mp

top_down_rules.title: Verify correct definition of the partition function
top_down_rules.description: The partition function Z is defined as the sum over all states of the system, where each state's Boltzmann factor is exp(-E_i / kT). It serves as the basis for calculating thermodynamic quantities.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure Z = Σ(exp(-E_i / kT)) is used, where the summation covers all possible states of the system.
common_errors: Omitting some states in the summation.
Using an incorrect Boltzmann factor, such as exp(E_i / kT) or exp(-kT / E_i).
Confusing the partition function for a probability distribution.

top_down_rules.title: Check dimensional consistency of the partition function
top_down_rules.description: The partition function Z must be dimensionless since it is a ratio of probabilities, ensuring compatibility with thermodynamic and statistical physics principles.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that E_i is in units of energy, k is the Boltzmann constant, and T is in absolute temperature (Kelvin). Confirm Z is a dimensionless quantity.
common_errors: Using non-energy units for E_i, such as momentum or force.
Incorrect units for k or T, leading to a non-dimensionless Z.
Forgetting to convert temperature to Kelvin when required.

top_down_rules.title: Ensure probability normalization using the partition function
top_down_rules.description: The probabilities of individual states, P_i = exp(-E_i / kT) / Z, must sum to 1 over all states. This ensures proper normalization in statistical mechanics.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check whether Σ(P_i) = 1, where P_i = exp(-E_i / kT) / Z and the summation spans all states.
common_errors: Forgetting to divide by the partition function Z.
Failing to include all states in the summation for normalization.
Incorrect exponentiation in the Boltzmann factor.

top_down_rules.title: Verify thermodynamic quantities derived from the partition function
top_down_rules.description: Thermodynamic quantities like internal energy (U), entropy (S), and Helmholtz free energy (F) are derived using derivatives of the partition function. For example, U = -∂(ln Z) / ∂(1/kT).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure the derivatives are correctly computed and consistent with the definitions of the thermodynamic quantities.
common_errors: Incorrect derivative of ln Z with respect to 1/kT.
Mixing up signs in the expressions for thermodynamic quantities.
Applying the derivative with respect to an incorrect variable (e.g., T instead of 1/kT).

top_down_rules.title: Check partition function behavior in the high-temperature limit
top_down_rules.description: In the high-temperature limit (T → ∞), the Boltzmann factor exp(-E_i / kT) approaches 1, and the partition function Z becomes approximately the total number of states.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that Z ≈ total number of states for T → ∞.
common_errors: Incorrect asymptotic behavior of Z in high-temperature conditions.
Ignoring the contribution of all states when summing in the high-temperature limit.

top_down_rules.title: Check partition function behavior in the low-temperature limit
top_down_rules.description: In the low-temperature limit (T → 0), the Boltzmann factor exp(-E_i / kT) is dominated by the ground state (lowest energy state). Thus, Z ≈ exp(-E_0 / kT).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that Z is dominated by the ground state contribution for T → 0.
common_errors: Failing to prioritize the ground state in the low-temperature limit.
Ignoring the behavior of the Boltzmann factor as T → 0.

top_down_rules.title: Verify validity conditions for using the partition function
top_down_rules.description: The partition function assumes the system is in thermal equilibrium and that the states are distinguishable and non-degenerate unless otherwise stated.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure the system is in thermal equilibrium and that the assumptions (e.g., distinguishability of states) are explicitly stated and valid.
common_errors: Applying the partition function to non-equilibrium systems.
Failing to account for degeneracy in the states when calculating Z.
Assuming indistinguishable particles without appropriate corrections.

top_down_rules.title: Verify relationship between Helmholtz free energy and partition function
top_down_rules.description: The Helmholtz free energy F is related to the partition function by F = -kT ln Z. This relationship connects statistical mechanics with thermodynamics.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure F = -kT ln Z is used correctly, with Z being dimensionless.
common_errors: Using a non-dimensionless Z in the logarithmic function.
Incorrect sign in the expression for F.
Using an incorrect base for the natural logarithm (e.g., log10 instead of ln).

top_down_rules.title: Apply Clausius-Clapeyron Equation
top_down_rules.description: The Clausius-Clapeyron equation describes the slope of the phase boundary in a pressure-temperature diagram for phase transitions. It applies when the transition is between phases in equilibrium with no external work done.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify the equation dP/dT = L/TV, where L is the latent heat and V is the change in volume, under equilibrium conditions.
common_errors: Incorrect differentiation of pressure with respect to temperature
Miscalculation of latent heat and volume change
Not considering the equilibrium condition

top_down_rules.title: Check units of latent heat
top_down_rules.description: Latent heat should be expressed in units consistent with energy per mass (e.g., J/kg or cal/g). Dimensional consistency is crucial for correct calculations.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure latent heat is given as energy per unit mass and consistently convert units where needed.
common_errors: Using energy units like joules without per mass unit
Incorrect conversion between calories and joules or between grams and kilograms
Ignoring units during calculation

top_down_rules.title: Verify entropy change during phase transition
top_down_rules.description: Entropy change should be calculated as S = L/T during a phase transition where the system is in thermal equilibrium.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the calculated S matches L/T, verifying that L is in proper energy units and T is in Kelvin.
common_errors: Wrong temperature unit; only Kelvin should be used
Neglecting the equilibrium condition resulting in incorrect entropy values
Incorrect calculations leading to negative entropy changes

top_down_rules.title: Determine correct sign for latent heat
top_down_rules.description: The sign of latent heat depends on the direction of the phase transition; positive for endothermic (e.g., melting) and negative for exothermic (e.g., freezing).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Identify the nature of the phase transition and verify that the sign of latent heat is correctly applied based on the transition direction.
common_errors: Using positive latent heat for exothermic transitions
Confusing the thermodynamic sign convention
Not defining the transition type clearly

top_down_rules.title: Consider constraints during critical phase transitions
top_down_rules.description: Critical points and phase transitions often involve boundary constraints such as volume, pressure, or temperature that require special consideration.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure calculations respect constraints specific to critical points, such as finite volume changes and constant temperature conditions.
common_errors: Ignoring boundary conditions at critical points
Misapplying constraints, leading to impossible physical states
Assuming linear behavior near critical transitions

top_down_rules.title: Verify phase diagram appropriateness
top_down_rules.description: Phase diagrams are only valid for well-characterized substances under equilibrium and standard conditions. Ensure assumptions match diagram representation.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Confirm phase diagram use fits documented equilibrium conditions and the material's properties.
common_errors: Using phase diagrams beyond their valid temperature-pressure range
Misinterpreting phase boundaries that have pressure-temperature dependencies
Assuming universal applicability without verification

top_down_rules.title: Check constraints for melting and boiling points
top_down_rules.description: Ensure temperature and pressure are controlled based on the material's melting and boiling points under specified conditions.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify melting/freezing and boiling/condensation calculations are performed with correct material data and consider standard atmospheric conditions where applicable.
common_errors: Assuming melting/boiling points at non-standard pressures or temperatures
Ignoring pressure variations in boiling calculations
Misusing ideal conditions when real data is required

top_down_rules.title: Verify conditions at the triple point
top_down_rules.description: The triple point is the unique set of conditions where three phases coexist in equilibrium. Test assumptions and data against this particular state.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure calculations and assumptions adhere to the specific temperature and pressure of a substance's triple point.
common_errors: Applying inappropriate conditions that deviate from the triple point's defined state
Misunderstanding the coexistence of phases at the triple point
Overlooking the exactness of triple point conditions in calculations

experience_rules.topic: Phase Transitions and Latent Heat
experience_rules.title: 流体静力平衡高度约束
experience_rules.trigger: 冰盖下存在液态水且达到静力学平衡时
experience_rules.check_logic: 检查是否满足冰压力等于水压力：ρi * g * H_ice = ρw * g * H_water。若不满足，水会流动直至平衡。

experience_rules.topic: Phase Transitions and Latent Heat
experience_rules.title: 相变体积收缩补偿规则
experience_rules.trigger: 涉及冰川/冰盖融化导致表面形变（凹陷）的建模时
experience_rules.check_logic: 需检查是否考虑了冰水密度差（ρi/ρw）导致的体积减小，以及该体积差与表面下沉体积（V_depression）的等量关系。

top_down_rules.title: Verify Positive Entropy Change for Irreversible Processes
top_down_rules.description: According to the second law of thermodynamics, entropy change must be greater than zero for irreversible processes.
top_down_rules.check_logic: If a process is identified as irreversible, verify that entropy change (ΔS) > 0. For reversible processes, ΔS = 0.
common_errors: Incorrectly calculating ΔS = 0 for irreversible processes
Using ΔS < 0 for spontaneous processes
Failing to distinguish between reversible and irreversible processes

top_down_rules.title: Entropy Dimensional Consistency
top_down_rules.description: Entropy must have the dimension of energy per temperature, typically joules per kelvin (J/K).
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure calculated entropy is expressed in units of J/K and verify dimensional consistency in calculations.
common_errors: Using incorrect units like J or K
Mixing units of power (Watts) with entropy
Failing to convert units properly in intermediate steps

top_down_rules.title: Confirm Maximum Efficiency for Carnot Cycle
top_down_rules.description: The efficiency of any cyclic heat engine cannot be greater than that of a Carnot cycle operating between the same high and low temperature reservoirs.
top_down_rules.check_logic: If a heat engine is compared against a Carnot engine, verify that η_engine ≤ η_Carnot = 1 - T_cold/T_hot, where temperatures are in absolute scale (Kelvin).
common_errors: Calculating η_engine > η_Carnot
Misidentifying T_cold and T_hot temperatures
Using temperatures in Celsius instead of Kelvin

top_down_rules.title: Adhere to Entropy Sign Convention
top_down_rules.description: The entropy change is positive for heat absorption and negative for heat rejection.
top_down_rules.check_logic: In processes involving heat transfer, ensure entropy change aligns with Q/T, where Q is heat absorbed (positive) or rejected (negative), and T is the absolute temperature.
common_errors: Confusing the sign of entropy change for heat absorbed vs. rejected
Neglecting to change sign when transitioning from absorption to rejection
Using incorrect temperature values for T

top_down_rules.title: Validate Boltzmann's Entropy Formula Application
top_down_rules.description: Boltzmann's entropy formula S = k ln(Ω) applies to systems in statistical equilibrium with a well-defined number of microstates.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure applicability of S = k ln(Ω) by verifying that the system is in equilibrium, Ω (number of microstates) is well-defined, and k is Boltzmann's constant.
common_errors: Applying Boltzmann's formula to non-equilibrium systems
Miscalculating Ω or ignoring its determination
Using incorrect value for Boltzmann's constant

top_down_rules.title: Confirm Zero Entropy Change in Adiabatic Processes
top_down_rules.description: In adiabatic processes without irreversibilities, the change in entropy should be zero.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check that for adiabatic processes (no heat exchange), ΔS = 0 unless internal irreversibilities are present. If irreversibilities exist, verify ΔS > 0.
common_errors: Assuming ΔS ≠ 0 for perfect adiabatic processes
Failing to identify presence of irreversibilities
Misinterpreting adiabatic processes as isothermal

top_down_rules.title: Assess Entropy Conservation in Isothermal Conditions
top_down_rules.description: During isothermal reversible processes, entropy changes are balanced such that ΔS_total = 0 for the system and surroundings.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure ΔS_system + ΔS_surroundings = 0 during a reversible isothermal process. Verify that heat transfer is consistent with Q/T for both system and surroundings.
common_errors: Ignoring entropy changes in surroundings during isothermal balancing
Misleading zero entropy system change as total entropy conservation
Failing to account for reversibility conditions

top_down_rules.title: Check Validity Conditions: Second Law Applications
top_down_rules.description: The second law applies universally for entropy considerations but is specifically valid for macroscopic systems in classical regimes. It cannot distinguish between microscopic fluctuations.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify application to classical, macroscopic systems and ensure that anomalies due to quantum or microscopic factors are not wrongly interpreted by the second law.
common_errors: Misapplication to quantum scale systems
Ignoring classical regime requirements in justification
Overlooking microscopic fluctuations in small systems

top_down_rules.title: Verify Entropy Behavior at Extremes
top_down_rules.description: Entropy approaches zero as temperature approaches absolute zero, consistent with the third law of thermodynamics.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that entropy calculations reflect S → 0 as T → 0 for perfect crystalline substances, and verify that entropy does not decrease below zero.
common_errors: Violating the third law by allowing negative entropy
Failing to account for residual entropy in non-perfect crystals
Incorrectly extrapolating entropy behavior at low temperatures

top_down_rules.title: Verify Correct Usage of Specific Heat Capacity Equation
top_down_rules.description: The specific heat capacity equation is Q = m*c*ΔT, where Q is the heat added, m is the mass, c is the specific heat capacity, and ΔT is the change in temperature.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that the equation Q = m*c*ΔT is correctly applied with the appropriate variables in the computation. Verify that all variables are substituted correctly and that the equation is used in the proper context.
common_errors: Incorrectly substituting mass (m) or specific heat capacity (c)
Confusing units of temperature change ΔT (use degrees Celsius or Kelvin consistently)

top_down_rules.title: Check Dimensional Consistency in Heat Capacity Calculations
top_down_rules.description: In calculations involving specific heat capacities, units must be consistent across the variables involved: Joules (J) for heat, kilograms (kg) for mass, and degrees Celsius (or Kelvin) for temperature.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify that dimensions match correctly: [Q] = Joules, [m] = kg, [c] = J/(kg·°C), [ΔT] = °C or K. Ensure proper unit conversions if necessary.
common_errors: Using calories instead of joules without conversion
Mismatch of units for mass or temperature
Mixing Kelvin and Celsius inconsistently

top_down_rules.title: Ensure Correct Sign Convention for Heat Flow
top_down_rules.description: Heat absorbed by the system should be positive, and heat released by the system should be negative.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check whether heat energy Q is assigned the correct sign based on the flow direction. Verify that endothermic and exothermic processes are correctly identified.
common_errors: Using incorrect sign for heat absorbed/released
Confusing endothermic and exothermic processes

top_down_rules.title: Ensure Valid Application of Constant Specific Heat
top_down_rules.description: Specific heat capacity is often assumed constant over small temperature changes. This assumption breaks down over larger ranges or near phase transitions.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Verify if the assumption that specific heat capacity is constant is valid for the given temperature range. Check for any phase transitions that may invalidate this assumption.
common_errors: Incorrect assumption of constant specific heat capacity over a large temperature range
Ignoring phase transitions

top_down_rules.title: Check for Conditions of Adiabatic Process
top_down_rules.description: An adiabatic process involves no heat exchange with the surroundings; only changes in internal energy occur.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that Q = 0 in adiabatic processes and focus on changes in pressure, volume, and internal energy. Verify that the first law of thermodynamics is applied correctly.
common_errors: Incorrectly adding heat in adiabatic processes
Misinterpreting adiabatic conditions

top_down_rules.title: Verify Applicability of Heat Capacity Ratio (γ)
top_down_rules.description: The heat capacity ratio, γ = Cp/Cv, applies specifically to ideal gases under adiabatic processes.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Ensure that γ is used only for ideal gases and is linked to the relation between specific heats under adiabatic conditions. Verify that Cp and Cv are correctly identified and used.
common_errors: Using γ in non-ideal gas scenarios
Misapplying Cp for Cv
Using γ in non-adiabatic processes

top_down_rules.title: Ensure Correct Conditions for Phase Transition Heat Calculations
top_down_rules.description: During phase transitions, specific latent heat (e.g., heat of fusion or vaporization) must be used instead of specific heat capacity.
top_down_rules.check_logic: Check if latent heat calculations are correctly applied during phase transitions. Ensure that the heat added or removed corresponds to the latent heat of the substance.
common_errors: Using specific heat capacity instead of latent heat
Ignoring heat absorbed or released during phase change
